# Gaussian statistics for left and right eigenvectors of complex non-Hermitian matrices

**Authors:** Sofiia Dubova ††thanks: Department of Mathematics, Harvard University Kevin Yang††footnotemark: Horng-Tzer Yau††footnotemark: Jun Yin ††thanks: Department of Mathematics, University of California, Los Angeles

## Abstract

We consider a constant-size subset of left and right eigenvectors of an $N\times N$ i.i.d. complex non-Hermitian matrix associated with the eigenvalues with pairwise distances at least $N^{-\frac{1}{2}+\epsilon}$ . We show that arbitrary constant rank projections of these eigenvectors are Gaussian and jointly independent.

## 1 Introduction

Eigenvector statistics of random matrix ensembles have been extensively studied in random matrix theory. In the case of Hermitian random matrices, which can be viewed as Hamiltonians of disordered quantum systems, the Quantum Unique Ergodicity (QUE) conjecture [34] asserts that their eigenvectors tend to be distributed uniformly on a sphere. For Gaussian orthogonal and Gaussian unitary ensembles this statement is trivially correct due to their invariance under multiplication by orthogonal and unitary matrices respectively. A great deal of work has been done to show that the behavior of the eigenvectors of (generalized) Wigner ensemble is consistent with QUE: delocalization of eigenvectors [21], asymptotic normality and independence of finitely many deterministic projections of eigenvectors [9, 30], the size and normality of other eigenvector statistics [14, 16, 6, 5]. Similar results have been established for other Hermitian ensembles in [10, 8, 1].

In the case of non-Hermitian i.i.d. ensembles, less is known. The delocalization of the eigenvectors has been established in [32, 33, 3, 4, 27, 28]. Some work has been done on the size and distribution of the overlaps $\mathcal{O}_{ij}=\langle u_{j},u_{i}\rangle\langle v_{i},v_{j}\rangle$ , where $u_{i},u_{j}$ and $v_{i},v_{j}$ are the right and left eigenvectors of a non-Hermitian i.i.d. matrix $A$ , see e.g. [7, 12, 19]. Overlaps $\mathcal{O}_{ij}$ are of particular interest for the non-Hermitian models as they govern [7, 24] the evolution of eigenvalues and eigenvectors of $A_{t}$ under the flow $\mathrm{d}A_{t}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\mathrm{d}B_{t}$ , where $B_{t}$ is a Brownian motion. In this work we obtain the Gaussianity of the deterministic projections of eigenvectors of $A$ .

The standard process for proving Gaussianity of the eigenvector statistics for a Hermitian ensemble $H$ is the well-known three-step strategy, initially used for the local eigenvalue statistics in [20]:

- 1. Local laws for the resolvent of $H$ ;

- 2. Gaussianity of the eigenvector statistics of a Gaussian divisible ensemble $H_{t}=H+\sqrt{t}B$ , where $B$ is GOE;

- 3. Comparison of the eigenvector statistics of the initial ensemble $H$ and $H_{t}$ .

The key component of this argument is the second step, which is done using the Eigenvector Moment Flow (EMF), first developed in [9]. EMF is derived from the evolution of eigenvectors under the flow $\mathrm{d}H_{t}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\mathrm{d}B_{t}$ , where $B_{t}$ is a standard Hermitian Brownian motion. The non-Hermitian analogue of this eigenvector evolution is a lot more complicated, see e.g. [7, 24].

In this paper we take a different approach to the second step of the three-step strategy. Our method is inspired by the supersymmetric approach recently used to prove the universality of local eigenvalue statistics of complex i.i.d. non-Hermitian matrices in the bulk in [29] and extended to the real case in [18, 31]. This method allows us to compute the moment generating functions of the eigenvector statistics of the Gaussian divisible ensemble $A+\sqrt{t}B$ directly through asymptotic analysis of the exact integral formulas for these functions at the time-scale $t=N^{-\frac{1}{3}+\epsilon_{0}}$ .

Some of the details behind the third step for non-Hermitian matrices are also different from what is done the Hermitian case [25]. As in [29], this comparison is done through Girko’s formula, and this requires translating eigenvector statistics into eigenvalue statistics in some sense. More is explained towards the end of the introduction.

Now we state the main result of this paper.

#### Theorem 1.

Let $A$ be an $N\times N$ complex random matrix with i.i.d. entries satisfying $\mathbb{E}A_{ij}=0$ , $\mathbb{E}\left|A_{ij}\right|^{2}=N^{-1}$ and $\mathbb{E}\left|A_{ij}\right|^{p}\leq C_{p}N^{-p/2}$ . Fix $\epsilon,\tau>0$ , $m_{R},m_{L}\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}$ , set $m=m_{R}+m_{L}$ . Consider deterministic points in the complex plane $\left\{z^{0}_{j}=z^{0}_{j}(N)\right\}_{j=1}^{m}\subset\mathbb{C}$ such that $\left|z^{0}_{j}\right|<1-\tau$ for any $1\leq j\leq m$ and $\left|z^{0}_{j}-z^{0}_{k}\right|\geq N^{-1/2+\epsilon}$ for any distinct $1\leq j,k\leq m$ . Let $(\lambda_{j},u_{j})$ denote an eigenvalue and the corresponding right eigenvector of $A$ for $1\leq j\leq m_{R}$ and $(\lambda_{j},v_{j})$ denote an eigenvalue and the corresponding left eigenvector of $A$ for $m_{R}+1\leq j\leq m$ . Let $\left\{T_{j}=T_{j}(N)\right\}_{j=1}^{m}$ be a family of deterministic bounded rank matrices with bounded norm. Then for any test function $F\in C_{c}^{\infty}\left(\mathbb{C}^{m}\times\mathbb{R}^{m}\right)$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{N\rightarrow\infty}\mathbb{E}F\left(\sqrt{N}(\lambda_{1}-z^{0}_{1}),\ldots,\sqrt{N}(\lambda_{m}-z^{0}_{m}),\|T_{1}u_{1}\|^{2},\ldots,\|T_{m}v_{m}\|^{2}\right) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\lim_{N\rightarrow\infty}\mathbb{E}F\left(\sqrt{N}(\lambda_{1}-z^{0}_{1}),\ldots,\sqrt{N}(\lambda_{m}-z^{0}_{m}),Z_{1}^{2},\ldots,Z_{m}^{2}\right), $$

where $Z=(Z_{1},\ldots,Z_{N})$ consists of independent Gaussian random variables $Z_{j}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\|T_{j}\|_{F}^{2})$ which are independent of $A$ .

Theorem 1 implies convergence in distribution of $\|T_{1}u_{1}\|^{2},\ldots,\|T_{m}v_{m}\|^{2}$ to squares of independent Gaussians. The point of including $\sqrt{N}(\lambda_{1}-z_{1}^{0}),\ldots,\sqrt{N}(\lambda_{m}-z_{m}^{0})$ is to pin down the corresponding eigenvalues near $z_{1}^{0},\ldots,z_{m}^{0}$ . Based on the universality result for local eigenvalue statistics in Theorem 1.2 of [29] (and its proof), we anticipate that

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{N\rightarrow\infty}\mathbb{E}F\left(\sqrt{N}(\lambda_{1}-z^{0}_{1}),\ldots,\sqrt{N}(\lambda_{m}-z^{0}_{m}),Z_{1}^{2},\ldots,Z_{m}^{2}\right) \displaystyle=\int_{\mathbb{C}^{m}}\mathbb{E}F(w_{1},\ldots,w_{m},Z_{1}^{2},\ldots,Z_{m}^{2})\rho_{\mathrm{GinUE}}^{(m)}(w_{1},\ldots,w_{m})\mathrm{d}w_{1}\ldots\mathrm{d}w_{m}, $$

where the expectation in the second line is with respect to $Z_{1},\ldots,Z_{m}$ , and

$$ \displaystyle\rho_{\mathrm{GinUE}}^{(m)}(w_{1},\ldots,w_{m})=\det\left[\frac{1}{\pi}e^{-\frac{1}{2}(|w_{j}|^{2}+|w_{\ell}|^{2})+w_{j}\overline{w}_{\ell}}\right]_{j,\ell=1}^{m}. $$

(We can assume that $z_{j}^{0}$ converge as $N\to\infty$ by taking a subsequence and observe that the limiting $m$ -point correlation function $\rho_{\mathrm{GinUE}}^{(m)}$ in Theorem 1.2 of [29] is independent of said limits of $z_{j}^{0}$ .) This should follow exactly from the proof of Theorem 1.2 in [29], but we have stated Theorem 1 in the above way since this argument is not written down.

As mentioned above, the proof of Theorem 1 follows the three-step strategy. The first step is carried out in [3, 17, 15, 12], where the authors establish the local laws for the resolvent of the Hermitization of $A$ :

$$ G_{z}(\eta)=\begin{pmatrix}-i\eta&A-z\\
A^{\ast}-\bar{z}&-i\eta\end{pmatrix}^{-1}. $$

In particular, the results we use in our proof are the averaged and isotropic local laws as well as the two-resolvent averaged local laws with possibly different shifts $z_{1}$ and $z_{2}$ . The second step is covered in Sections 2-6. Here we adapt the method of [29] to access left and right eigenvectors. The first technical aspect of this step is analyzing the resolvents $[(A-z)^{\ast}(A-z)+\eta^{2}+Y]^{-1}$ and $[(A-z)(A-z)^{\ast}+\eta^{2}+Y]^{-1}$ , where $Y$ is finite rank, Hermitian, and possibly negative. The method of [29] depends crucially on various positivity properties and estimates for the resolvents when $Y=0$ . We must ensure these properties are stable under perturbation by $Y$ ; this is why we require isotropic local laws in addition to the estimates used in [29]. Moreover, when studying multiple eigenvalues, we must also analyze these resolvents after projecting to the orthogonal complement of the span of finitely many eigenvectors. Isotropic local laws for deterministic vectors alone no longer suffice. We must also remove the projection using various perturbations and the concentration estimates in Section 6 of [29] (this is the content of Section 6).

The third step, the comparison between the eigenvector statistics of a general i.i.d. matrix and a Gaussian divisible matrix, is done in Sections 7 and 8. This argument follows the same framework as the eigenvector comparison argument of [25] for the Hermitian matrices. The key novelty of our proof is the approximation of the eigenvector statistics with certain functions of $G^{z}$ in Lemma 21 and Girko’s formula [23]. This approximation relies on the level repulsion estimate for the singular values of $A-z$ in Proposition 23 that we derive using Theorem 2.10 of [19] and Theorem 3.2 of [11]. The rest of the argument is a standard Green function comparison, see e.g. [26].

### 1.1 Notation

We denote the standard basis vectors in $\mathbb{C}^{m}$ by $\mathbf{e}_{j,m}$ for $1\leq j\leq m$ . Whenever the dimension of the space is clear from the context we omit it and write $\mathbf{e}_{j}=\mathbf{e}_{j,m}$ . We write $\llbracket a,b\rrbracket=\mathbb{Z}\cap[a,b]$ . Given a matrix $X$ , normalized trace of $X$ is $\left\langle X\right\rangle=N^{-1}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}X$ .

## 2 Gaussian divisible matrices

In this section we state the main results for Gaussian divisible matrices. For any $A\in M_{N}(\mathbb{C})$ we define its Hermitization by

$$ \mathcal{H}_{z}=\begin{pmatrix}0&A-z\\
A^{\ast}-\bar{z}&0\end{pmatrix},\,z\in\mathbb{C}. $$

The resolvent of this Hermitization $G_{z}(\eta)=\left(\mathcal{H}_{z}-i\eta\right)^{-1}$ can be written as

$$ G_{z}(\eta)=\begin{pmatrix}i\eta\tilde{H}_{z}(\eta)&\tilde{H}_{z}(\eta)(A-z)\\
(A^{\ast}-\bar{z})\tilde{H}_{z}(\eta)&i\eta H_{z}(\eta)\end{pmatrix}, $$

where

$$ \displaystyle H_{z}(\eta) \displaystyle=\left[(A-z)^{\ast}(A-z)+\eta^{2}\right]^{-1}, \displaystyle\tilde{H}_{z}(\eta) \displaystyle=\left[(A-z)(A-z)^{\ast}+\eta^{2}\right]^{-1}. $$

We will now condition on some assumptions on $A$ ; we explain shortly why they hold with probability $1-O(N^{-D})$ for any $D>0$ . Consider $\epsilon_{0}>0$ . We assume that for any $\eta,\eta_{1},\eta_{2},\in[N^{-\frac{1}{2}+\epsilon_{0}},10]$ , $\eta^{\ast}=\max\{\eta_{1},\eta_{2}\}$ and $z,z_{1},z_{2}\in\mathbb{C}$ such that $|z|,|z_{1}|,|z_{2}|<1-\tau$ for some fixed $\tau>0$ , there exist constants $c=c(\epsilon_{0})>0$ and $C=C(\epsilon_{0})>0$ such that

#### A1:

We have

$$ \displaystyle c\eta^{-1}\leq\left\langle H_{z}(\eta)\right\rangle\leq C\eta^{-1}, \displaystyle c\eta^{-2}\leq\left\langle H_{z}(\eta)\tilde{H}_{z}(\eta)\right\rangle\leq C\eta^{-2}, \displaystyle\left|\left\langle H_{z}(\eta)^{2}(A-z)\right\rangle\right|\leq C\eta^{-1}, \displaystyle c\eta^{-3}\leq\left\langle H_{z}(\eta)^{2}\right\rangle\leq C\eta^{-3}. $$

For

$$ B_{j}=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\
0&0\end{pmatrix}\otimes I_{N}\text{ or }\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\
1&0\end{pmatrix}\otimes I_{N} $$

we have

$$ \displaystyle\left|\left\langle G_{z}(\eta_{1})B_{1}G_{z}(\eta_{2})B_{2}\right\rangle\right| \displaystyle\leq C. $$

#### A2:

We have

$$ \displaystyle\left\langle H_{z_{1}}(\eta_{1})H_{z_{2}}(\eta_{2})\right\rangle \displaystyle\geq c\left(\eta^{\ast}\right)^{-2}, \displaystyle\left\langle\tilde{H}_{z_{1}}(\eta_{1})\tilde{H}_{z_{2}}(\eta_{2})\right\rangle \displaystyle\geq c\left(\eta^{\ast}\right)^{-2}, \displaystyle\left\langle H_{z_{1}}(\eta_{1})\tilde{H}_{z_{2}}(\eta_{2})\right\rangle \displaystyle\geq\frac{c}{\eta^{\ast}\left(\eta^{\ast}+|z_{1}-z_{2}|^{2}\right)}. $$

We fix $m$ families of finite rank deterministic matrices $T_{j}$ , where $j\in\llbracket 1,m\rrbracket$ and $m\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}$ . Then matrices $T_{j}T_{j}^{\ast}$ have spectral decomposition

$$ \displaystyle T_{j}T_{j}^{\ast}=\sum_{k=1}^{l_{j}}q_{j,k}\mathbf{w}_{j,k}\mathbf{w}_{j,k}^{\ast}, $$

where $q_{j,k}$ are positive constants and $\{\mathbf{w}_{j,k}\}_{k}$ are deterministic orthonormal vectors for each $j$ . We make the following assumption on $A$ in relation to matrices $T_{j}$ .

#### A3:

For any $\mathbf{w}_{1},\mathbf{w}_{2}\in\left\{\mathbf{w}_{j,k_{1}},\mathbf{w}_{j,k_{1}}\pm\mathbf{w}_{j,k_{2}},\mathbf{w}_{j,k_{1}}\pm i\mathbf{w}_{j,k_{2}}\right\}_{j\in\llbracket 1,m\rrbracket,k_{1},k_{2}\in\llbracket 1,l_{j}\rrbracket}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\left|\mathbf{w}_{1}^{\ast}H_{z}(\eta)\mathbf{w}_{2}-\left\langle H_{z}(\eta)\right\rangle\mathbf{w}_{1}^{\ast}\mathbf{w}_{2}\right|\leq C\eta^{-\frac{3}{2}}N^{-\frac{1}{2}}, \displaystyle\left|\mathbf{w}_{1}^{\ast}\tilde{H}_{z}(\eta)\mathbf{w}_{2}-\left\langle\tilde{H}_{z}(\eta)\right\rangle\mathbf{w}_{1}^{\ast}\mathbf{w}_{2}\right|\leq C\eta^{-\frac{3}{2}}N^{-\frac{1}{2}}. $$

Let us explain why assumptions A1, A2, A3 hold for i.i.d. matrices $A$ with probability $1-O(N^{-D})$ for any $D>0$ fixed. All of A1 is explained in Section 7 of [29]; see after Lemma 7.1 in [29]. For A2, see (8.3)-(8.5). For A3, see Proposition 29.

Now, following [29], for any $z\in\mathbb{C}$ such that $|z|<1$ and $t>0$ , we define $\eta_{z,t}>0$ such that $t\langle H_{z}(\eta_{z,t})\rangle=1$ . By (A1.1), we know $ct\leq\eta_{z,t}\leq Ct$ for finite constants $C,c>0$ for all $|z|<1-\tau$ and $t\geq N^{-1/2+\epsilon}$ . (The existence and uniqueness of such $\eta_{z,t}$ for $|z|<1$ and $t\geq N^{-1/2+\epsilon}$ holds by Theorem 1.1 in [29].)

#### Theorem 2.

Suppose $t=N^{-\frac{1}{3}+\epsilon_{0}}$ for some $\epsilon_{0}>0$ fixed. Let $m_{R},m_{L}\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}$ . For any $j\in\llbracket 1,m_{R}\rrbracket$ let $(\lambda_{j},u_{j})$ denote an eigenvalue-right-eigenvector pair of $M_{t}$ , and for any $j\in\llbracket m_{R}+1,m_{R}+m_{L}\rrbracket$ let $(\lambda_{j},v_{j})$ denote an eigenvalue-left-eigenvector pair of $M_{t}$ . Assume that there exists $\upsilon>0$ such that $|\lambda_{j}-\lambda_{k}|\geq N^{-1/2+\upsilon}$ for any distinct $j,k\in\llbracket 1,m_{R}\rrbracket$ and for any distinct $j,k\in\llbracket m_{R}+1,m_{R}+m_{L}\rrbracket$ . Let $\{T_{j}\}_{j\in\llbracket 1,m_{R}+m_{L}\rrbracket}$ be deterministic, finite-rank matrices. There exists $\kappa>0$ and $\mathfrak{q}>0$ depending only on $T_{1},\ldots,T_{m_{R}+m_{L}}$ such that for all $q_{1},\ldots,q_{m_{R}+m_{L}}<\mathfrak{q}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\bm{\lambda}}\prod_{j=1}^{m_{R}}\exp[Nq_{j}\|T_{j}u_{j}\|^{2}]\prod_{j=m_{R}+1}^{m_{R}+m_{L}}\exp[Nq_{j}\|T_{j}v_{j}\|^{2}] \displaystyle=\prod_{j=1}^{m}\det[1-tq_{j}H_{\lambda_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})T_{j}^{\ast}T_{j}]^{-1}\left[1+O(N^{-\kappa})\right]. $$

Above, $\mathbb{E}_{\bm{\lambda}}$ denotes expectation conditioning on $\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{m_{R}+m_{L}}$ .

The choice $t=N^{-\frac{1}{3}+\epsilon}$ can perhaps be improved to $t=N^{-\frac{1}{2}+\epsilon}$ , or even $t=N^{-1+\epsilon}$ ; see the end of Section 1 in [29]. For this reason, often in the proof we use only the lower bounds $t\geq N^{-1/2+\epsilon}$ .

Theorem 2 gives joint normality in the large $N$ limit of finitely many components of finitely many left and right eigenvectors (subject to a separation condition on eigenvalues for eigenvectors on the same side, right or left). This is the content of the following result.

#### Corollary 3.

The random vector $(N\|T_{j}u_{j}\|^{2},N\|T_{k}v_{k}\|^{2})_{j,k}$ converges in distribution to $(Z_{j}^{2},Z_{k}^{2})_{j,k}$ , where $Z_{j}\sim N(0,\|T_{j}\|_{\mathrm{F}}^{2})$ are independent (here, $\|\cdot\|_{\mathrm{F}}$ is the Frobenius norm for square matrices).

#### Proof.

By Theorem 2, it suffices to show that for the above choices of $T_{j}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\det[1-tq_{j}H_{\lambda_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})T_{j}^{\ast}T_{j}]^{-1}=[1-tq_{j}\|T_{j}\|_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}]^{-1}[1+O(N^{-\kappa})] $$

for small enough $q_{j}>0$ and for some $\kappa>0$ . To this end, we claim

$$ \displaystyle\det[1-tq_{j}H_{\lambda_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})T_{j}^{\ast}T_{j}]^{-1} \displaystyle=\prod_{k=1}^{\ell_{j}}[1-tq_{j}q_{j,k}\mathbf{w}_{j,k}^{\ast}H_{\lambda_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})\mathbf{w}_{j,k}]^{-1}\left[1+O(N^{-\kappa})\right] \displaystyle=\prod_{k=1}^{\ell_{j}}[1-q_{j}q_{j,k}\|\mathbf{w}_{j,k}\|^{2}]^{-1}\left[1+O(N^{-\kappa})\right] \displaystyle=[1-tq_{j}\|T_{j}\|_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}]^{-1}[1+O(N^{-\kappa})], $$

where vectors $\mathbf{w}_{j,k}$ and scalars $q_{j,k}$ are defined by (2.1). The second line holds by (A3.1) and $t=\langle H_{\lambda_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})\rangle$ . It suffices to show the first line. To this end, for any $j$ , define the vectors

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{x}_{j,k}=q_{j,k}^{\frac{1}{2}}H_{\lambda_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})^{1/2}\mathbf{w}_{j,k} $$

and let $\{\mathbf{y}_{j,k}\}$ be the collection of orthogonal vectors obtained by Gram-Schmidt applied to $\{\mathbf{x}_{j,k}\}_{k}$ without dividing by the norm. In particular, we have

$$ \displaystyle\det[1-tq_{j}H_{\lambda_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})T_{j}^{\ast}T_{j}]^{-1} \displaystyle=\det\left[1-tq_{j}\sum_{k=1}^{\ell_{j}}\mathbf{x}_{j,k}\mathbf{x}_{j,k}^{\ast}\right]^{-1}=\prod_{k=1}^{\ell_{j}}[1-tq_{j}\mathbf{y}_{j,k}^{\ast}\mathbf{y}_{j,k}]^{-1}. $$

By (A1.1) and (A3.1), we know $\mathbf{x}_{j,k}^{\ast}\mathbf{x}_{j,m}=O(N^{-1/2}t^{-3/2})$ if $k\neq m$ and $C^{-1}t^{-1}\leq|\mathbf{x}_{j,k}|^{2}\leq Ct^{-1}$ for some $C>0$ . It follows by Gram-Schmidt that $\mathbf{y}_{j,k}^{\ast}\mathbf{y}_{j,k}=\mathbf{x}_{j,k}^{\ast}\mathbf{x}_{j,k}[1+O(N^{-1/2}t^{-1/2})]$ . Thus,

$$ \displaystyle\prod_{k=1}^{\ell_{j}}[1-tq_{j}\mathbf{y}_{j,k}^{\ast}\mathbf{y}_{j,k}]^{-1} \displaystyle=\prod_{k=1}^{\ell_{j}}[1-tq_{j}\mathbf{x}_{j,k}^{\ast}\mathbf{x}_{j,k}(1+O(N^{-1/2}t^{-1/2})]^{-1} \displaystyle=\prod_{k=1}^{\ell_{j}}[1-tq_{j}q_{j,k}\mathbf{w}_{j,k}^{\ast}H_{\lambda_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})\mathbf{w}_{j,k}(1+O(N^{-1/2}t^{-1/2})]^{-1}. $$

By (A3.1) and $t\geq N^{-1/3+\epsilon_{0}}$ and $t\langle H_{\lambda_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})\rangle=1$ , we know for some $\kappa>0$ that

$$ \displaystyle tq_{j}q_{j,k}\mathbf{w}_{j,k}^{\ast}H_{\lambda_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})\mathbf{w}_{j,k} \displaystyle=tq_{j}q_{j,k}\left[\langle H_{\lambda_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})\rangle+O(N^{-1/2}t^{-3/2})\right] \displaystyle=q_{j}q_{j,k}\left[1+O(N^{-1/2}t^{-1/2})\right]=q_{j}q_{j,k}[1+O(N^{-\kappa})]. $$

In particular, since $q_{j},q_{j,k}\neq 0$ and $|q_{j}|$ is small, this implies that

$$ \displaystyle[1-tq_{j}q_{j,k}\mathbf{w}_{j,k}^{\ast}H_{\lambda_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})\mathbf{w}_{j,k}(1+O(N^{-1/2}t^{-1/2})]^{-1} \displaystyle=[1-tq_{j}q_{j,k}\mathbf{w}_{j,k}^{\ast}H_{\lambda_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})\mathbf{w}_{j,k}]^{-1}(1+O(N^{-1/2}t^{-1/2}), $$

which completes the proof. ∎

The first main step to prove Theorem 2 is the case where $m_{R}+m_{L}=1$ . The second is the case $q_{1},\ldots,q_{m_{R}+m_{L}}\leq q$ , where we have a priori bounds of the form $\exp[Nq_{j}\|T_{j}u_{j}\|^{2}]\leq 1$ .

#### Proposition 4.

Suppose $t=N^{-\frac{1}{3}+\epsilon_{0}}$ for some $\epsilon_{0}>0$ fixed. Let $(\lambda_{1},u)$ denote an eigenvalue-right-eigenvector pair of $M_{t}$ , and let $T$ be a fixed deterministic finite rank matrix. There exists $\kappa>0$ and $q_{T}>0$ such that for all $q<q_{T}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\lambda_{1}}\exp[Nq\|Tu\|^{2}]=\frac{1}{\det[1-tqH_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})T^{\ast}T]}\left[1+O(N^{-\kappa})\right]. $$

Let $(\lambda_{2},v)$ denote an eigenvalue-left-eigenvector pair of $M_{t}$ , and let $T$ be a fixed deterministic finite rank matrix. There exists $\kappa>0$ and $q_{T}>0$ such that for all $q<q_{T}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\lambda_{2}}\exp[Nq\|Tv\|^{2}]=\frac{1}{\det[1-tq\tilde{H}_{\lambda_{2}}(\eta_{\lambda_{2},t})T^{\ast}T]}\left[1+O(N^{-\kappa})\right]. $$

#### Proposition 5.

Retain the setting of Theorem 2. Then (2.2) holds for all $q_{1},\dots,q_{m_{R}+m_{L}}\leq 0$ .

#### Proof of Theorem 2.

Proposition 4 implies the term inside the expectation in (2.2) (for small enough $q_{j}$ ) is tight as $N\to\infty$ , and its expectation converges along subsequences to that of its subsequential limits. Proposition 5 identifies these subsequential limits. ∎

## 3 Change of variables

In this section, we prepare the necessary change of variables for multiple left/right eigenvectors. For any positive integer $j$ consider a manifold

$$ \displaystyle\Omega_{j}=\mathbb{C}\times\mathbb{S}^{N-j}\times\mathbb{C}^{N-j}. $$

We define Householder transformations $R_{j}:\mathbb{S}^{N-j}\to\mathbf{U}(N-j+1)$ via

$$ \displaystyle R_{j}(u) \displaystyle=I_{N-j+1}-2\frac{(\mathbf{e}_{1}-u)(\mathbf{e}_{1}-u)^{\ast}}{\|\mathbf{e}_{1}-u\|^{2}}. $$

Now, define the maps

$$ \displaystyle\Phi_{j}^{R},\Phi_{j}^{L}:\Omega_{j}\times M_{N-j}(\mathbb{C})\rightarrow M_{N-j+1}(\mathbb{C}) $$

given by the data

$$ \displaystyle\Phi_{j}^{R}(\lambda_{j},u^{(j-1)},w_{j},M^{(j)}) \displaystyle=R_{j}(u^{(j-1)})\begin{pmatrix}\lambda_{j}&w_{j}^{\ast}\\
0&M^{(j)}\end{pmatrix}R_{j}(u^{(j-1)}), \displaystyle\Phi_{j}^{L}(\lambda_{j},v^{(j-1)},w_{j},M^{(j)}) \displaystyle=R_{j}(v^{(j-1)})\begin{pmatrix}\lambda_{j}&0\\
w_{j}&M^{(j)}\end{pmatrix}R_{j}(v^{(j-1)}). $$

Finally, consider a map

$$ \Phi:\prod_{j=1}^{m_{R}+m_{L}}\Omega_{j}\times M_{N-m_{R}-m_{L}}(\mathbb{C})\rightarrow M_{N}(\mathbb{C}) $$

given by the composition of several $\Phi_{j}^{R}$ and $\Phi_{j}^{L}$ maps

$$ \Phi=\Phi_{1}^{R}\circ\left(\mathrm{Id}\times\Phi_{2}^{R}\right)\circ\ldots\circ\left(\mathrm{Id}\times\Phi_{m_{R}}^{R}\right)\circ\left(\mathrm{Id}\times\Phi_{m_{R}+1}^{L}\right)\circ\ldots\circ\left(\mathrm{Id}\times\Phi_{m_{R}+m_{L}}^{L}\right). $$

For brevity we denote the total number of steps by $m=m_{R}+m_{L}$ .

#### Lemma 6.

The Jacobian of $\Phi$ is given by the following:

$$ \displaystyle J(\Phi)=|\Delta(\bm{\lambda})|^{2}\prod_{j=1}^{m}|\det[\lambda_{j}-M^{(m)}]|^{2}. $$

#### Proof.

Since $\Phi$ is the composition of several $\Phi_{j}^{R}$ and $\Phi_{j}^{L}$ maps, we have the chain rule

$$ J(\Phi)=\prod_{j=1}^{m_{R}}J(\Phi_{j}^{R})\prod_{j=m_{R}+1}^{m}J(\Phi_{j}^{L}). $$

We now claim that

$$ \displaystyle J(\Phi_{j}^{R})=J(\Phi_{j}^{L})=\left|\det[\lambda_{j}-M^{(j)}]\right| $$

for $j\in\llbracket 1,m\rrbracket$ . For the maps $\Phi_{j}^{R}$ , this holds by Lemma 3.1 of [29]. For the maps $\Phi_{j}^{L}$ , we use Lemma 3.1 in [29] (this lemma holds for left eigenvectors as well, since one can always replace $M^{(j-1)}$ , for which we apply Lemma 3.1 of [29], by its adjoint). It remains to note

## 4 Proof of Proposition 4

We prove (2.3), since (2.4) follows by the same argument (just replace $A$ by $A^{\ast}$ to make left eigenvectors into right eigenvectors; in particular, this is why (2.4) has $\tilde{H}$ instead of $H$ ). Now, to compute $\mathbb{E}_{\lambda}\exp[Nq\|Tu\|^{2}]$ , we use (3.2) and integrate out everything except $u$ (equivalently, set $m=m_{R}=1$ in our application of (3.2)). This gives the formula

where $\approx$ means true up to a factor of $1+O(N^{-\delta})$ for $\delta>0$ , and where

$$ \displaystyle K_{q} \displaystyle:=\int_{\mathbb{S}^{N-1}}e^{-\frac{N}{t}u^{\ast}[(A-\lambda_{1})^{\ast}(A-\lambda_{1})+\eta_{\lambda_{1},t}^{2}-tqT^{\ast}T]u}\mathrm{d}u, \displaystyle\mathrm{d}\mu_{q}(u) \displaystyle:=K_{q}^{-1}e^{-\frac{N}{t}u^{\ast}[(A-\lambda_{1})^{\ast}(A-\lambda_{1})+\eta_{\lambda_{1},t}^{2}-tqT^{\ast}T]u}\mathrm{d}u. $$

Before we can further analyze $K_{q}$ and the other remaining terms, we need a preliminary estimate. For convenience, let us the use the notation $H_{\lambda,q}(\eta):=[(A-\lambda)^{\ast}(A-\lambda)+\eta^{2}-tqT^{\ast}T]^{-1}$ . Note that $H_{\lambda,0,T}(\eta):=H_{\lambda}(\eta)$ . Let us also use the following more general notation, since it will be important for the proof of Proposition 5. For any $j\geq 0$ , recall $A^{(j)}$ . Define

$$ \displaystyle H_{\lambda,q}^{(j)}(\eta) \displaystyle:=[(A^{(j)}-\lambda)^{\ast}(A^{(j)}-\lambda)+\eta^{2}-tqT^{\ast}T]^{-1}, \displaystyle\tilde{H}_{\lambda,q,T}^{(j)}(\eta) \displaystyle:=[(A^{(j)}-\lambda)(A^{(j)}-\lambda)^{\ast}+\eta^{2}-tqT^{\ast}T]^{-1} $$

We also define $H_{\lambda}^{(j)}(\eta):=H_{\lambda,0,T}^{(j)}(\eta)$ and $\tilde{H}_{\lambda}^{(j)}(\eta):=H_{\lambda,0,T}^{(j)}(\eta)$ . Here, we always assume that $T$ has the same dimension as $A^{(j)}$ , and that $T$ is finite rank.

#### Lemma 7.

Fix $\lambda\in\mathbb{C}$ . There exists $q_{T}>0$ such that if $q<q_{T}$ , then for some finite-rank, positive semi-definite Hermitian matrix $Y$ with operator norm $\|Y\|_{\mathrm{op}}=O(1)$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle H_{\lambda,q}^{(j)}(\eta_{\lambda,t})=H_{\lambda}^{(j)}(\eta_{\lambda,t})^{\frac{1}{2}}[I+qY]H_{\lambda}^{(j)}(\eta_{\lambda,t})^{\frac{1}{2}}. $$

Moreover, we have $\langle H_{\lambda,q}^{(j)}(\eta_{\lambda,t})\rangle=\langle H_{\lambda}^{(j)}(\eta_{\lambda,t})\rangle+O(N^{-1})$ . The same is true for $\tilde{H}$ in place of $H$ .

#### Proof.

We prove the claim for $H$ and not $\tilde{H}$ ; for $\tilde{H}$ , again, the same argument applies (just replace $A$ by $A^{\ast}$ ). Also, We first assume $j=0$ ; we comment on general $j$ at the end. Recall $C^{-1}t\leq\eta_{\lambda,t}\leq Ct$ for some $C>0$ . By the Woodbury matrix identity, we have

$$ \displaystyle H_{\lambda,q}(\eta_{\lambda,t}) \displaystyle=H_{\lambda}(\eta_{\lambda,t})+H_{\lambda}(\eta_{\lambda,t})T^{\ast}[t^{-1}q^{-1}-TH_{\lambda}(\eta_{\lambda,t})T^{\ast}]^{-1}TH_{\lambda}(\eta_{\lambda,t}). $$

By (A1.1) and (A3.1), since $T^{\ast}T$ is a finite rank projection with $O(1)$ operator norm, we have $\|TH_{\lambda}(\eta_{\lambda,t})T^{\ast}\|_{\mathrm{op}}=O(t^{-1})$ . Hence, we can choose $q_{T}>0$ such that if $q<q_{T}$ , then the term in square brackets on the RHS is a Hermitian operator that is bounded below by $Cq^{-1}t^{-1}$ . In particular, the second term on the RHS of the above identity has the form $tqH_{\lambda}(\eta_{\lambda,t})T^{\ast}XTH_{\lambda}(\eta_{\lambda,t})$ with $X$ Hermitian, bounded, and positive, i.e.

$$ \displaystyle H_{\lambda,q}(\eta_{\lambda,t}) \displaystyle=H_{\lambda}(\eta_{\lambda,t})+tqH_{\lambda}(\eta_{\lambda,t})T^{\ast}XTH_{\lambda}(\eta_{\lambda,t}) \displaystyle=H_{\lambda}(\eta_{\lambda,t})^{\frac{1}{2}}\left\{I+tqH_{\lambda}(\eta_{\lambda,t})^{\frac{1}{2}}T^{\ast}XTH_{\lambda}(\eta_{\lambda,t})^{\frac{1}{2}}\right\}H_{\lambda}(\eta_{\lambda,t})^{\frac{1}{2}}. $$

To prove the first estimate, it suffices to show that the second term inside the curly brackets without the factor $q$ has operator norm $O(1)$ . This term is a finite rank, positive operator, so we can bound its operator norm by its trace. This gives

$$ \displaystyle\|tH_{\lambda}(\eta_{\lambda,t})^{\frac{1}{2}}T^{\ast}XTH_{\lambda}(\eta_{\lambda,t})^{\frac{1}{2}}\|_{\mathrm{op}} \displaystyle\leq t{\operatorname{Tr}\,}H_{\lambda}(\eta_{\lambda,t})^{\frac{1}{2}}T^{\ast}XTH_{\lambda}(\eta_{\lambda,t})^{\frac{1}{2}} \displaystyle=t{\operatorname{Tr}\,}TH_{\lambda}(\eta_{\lambda,t})T^{\ast}X \displaystyle\leq t\|X\|_{\mathrm{op}}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}TH_{\lambda}(\eta_{\lambda,t})T^{\ast}. $$

Again, we use (A1.1) and (A3.1) to get $t{\operatorname{Tr}\,}TH_{\lambda}(\eta_{\lambda,t})T^{\ast}=O(1)$ . Now use $\|X\|_{\mathrm{op}}=O(1)$ to get the first estimate. For the comparison of normalized traces, we have

$$ \displaystyle{\operatorname{Tr}\,}H_{\lambda}(\eta_{\lambda,t})^{\frac{1}{2}}T^{\ast}XTH_{\lambda}(\eta_{\lambda,t})^{\frac{1}{2}} \displaystyle={\operatorname{Tr}\,}TH_{\lambda}(\eta_{\lambda,t})T^{\ast}X \displaystyle=O(1){\operatorname{Tr}\,}TH_{\lambda}(\eta_{\lambda,t})T^{\ast}=O(t^{-1}); $$

the last line holds by $\|X\|_{\mathrm{op}}=O(1)$ , by (A1.1), and (A3.1), and by $\eta_{\lambda,t}^{-1}=O(t^{-1})$ . Multiply by $O(N^{-1}t)$ to conclude. For general $j\neq 0$ , the same argument works. Indeed, all we need are

$$ \displaystyle\|TH_{\lambda}^{(j)}(\eta_{\lambda,t})T^{\ast}\|_{\mathrm{op}}=O(t^{-1})\quad\mathrm{and}\quad{\operatorname{Tr}\,}TH_{\lambda}^{(j)}(\eta_{\lambda,t})T^{\ast}=O(t^{-1}). $$

The former follows from the latter. The latter follows by interlacing (and the corresponding estimate without the $(j)$ superscript). ∎

We proceed to analyze $K_{q}$ . By Lemma 7, we know $C^{-1}H_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})\leq H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})\leq CH_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})$ for a finite, positive constant $C$ . In particular, by Lemma 6.1 in [29], we have

$$ \displaystyle K_{q} \displaystyle=C_{N,t}\det[H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})]\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{i\frac{N}{t}p}\det[I+ipH_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})]^{-1}\mathrm{d}p. $$

The two-sided bound $C^{-1}H_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})\leq H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})\leq CH_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})$ is used in the proof of Lemma 6.1 of [29] only to guarantee that $H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})$ is strictly positive. We now use it to justify the following approximation (see immediately after the proof of Lemma 6.1 in [29]):

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{i\frac{N}{t}p}\det[I+ipH_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})]^{-1}\mathrm{d}p \displaystyle\approx\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{i\frac{N}{t}p}\exp\left\{-iNp\langle H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})\rangle-\frac{1}{2}Np^{2}\langle H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})^{2}\rangle\right\}\mathrm{d}p. $$

By the trace estimate in Lemma 7, we can continue as follows (below, $\kappa_{N,t,\lambda_{1}}=O(1)$ ):

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{i\frac{N}{t}p}\exp\left\{-iNp\langle H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})\rangle-\frac{1}{2}Np^{2}\langle H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})^{2}\rangle\right\}\mathrm{d}p \displaystyle=\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{i\frac{N}{t}p[1-t\langle H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})\rangle]}\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2}Np^{2}\langle H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})^{2}\rangle\right\}\mathrm{d}p \displaystyle=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\exp\left\{i\kappa_{N,t,\lambda_{1}}p\right\}\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2}Np^{2}\langle H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})^{2}\rangle\right\}\mathrm{d}p \displaystyle=\frac{\sqrt{2\pi}}{N^{1/2}\langle H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})^{2}\rangle^{1/2}}\exp\left\{-\frac{\kappa_{N,t,\lambda_{1}}^{2}}{2N\langle H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})^{2}\rangle}\right\}. $$

The last line follows by Gaussian Fourier transform. The bounds $C^{-1}H_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})\leq H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})$ and $\langle H_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},q})^{2}\rangle\geq C^{-1}\eta_{\lambda_{1},q}^{-3}$ and $\kappa_{N,t,\lambda_{1}}=O(1)$ show that the exponential in the last line is $\approx 1$ . Now, note that if $q\geq 0$ , then $H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})-H_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})\geq 0$ , and that if $q\leq 0$ , the reverse inequality holds. This follows by Lemma 7. In particular, $H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})-H_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})$ is always positive or negative semi-definite; it cannot have both positive and negative eigenvalues. Using this, we have the following, where the last line follows by $H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})\leq CH_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})$ and Lemma 7:

$$ \displaystyle|\langle H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})^{2}\rangle^{\frac{1}{2}}-\langle H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})^{2}\rangle^{\frac{1}{2}}|\lesssim|\langle H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})^{2}\rangle-\langle H_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})^{2}\rangle|^{\frac{1}{2}} \displaystyle\lesssim(\|H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\|H_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})\|_{\mathrm{op}})|\langle H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})-H_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})\rangle| \displaystyle\lesssim\|H_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})\|_{\mathrm{op}}||\langle H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})-H_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})\rangle|\lesssim N^{-1}t^{-2}. $$

Because $C^{-1}H_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})\leq H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})$ , we also have $\langle H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})^{2}\rangle^{1/2}\gtrsim\langle H_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})^{2}\rangle^{1/2}\gtrsim t^{-3/2}$ . Ultimately, since $\langle H_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})^{2}\rangle$ depends only on $N,t$ (recall that $\lambda_{1}$ is fixed), we have

$$ \displaystyle K_{q} \displaystyle=C_{N,t}\det[H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})]\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{i\frac{N}{t}p}\det[I+ipH_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})]^{-1}\mathrm{d}p\approx C_{N,t}\det[H_{\lambda_{1},q}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})]. $$

We now show (4.3)-(4.5). We give details for (4.3); it amounts to adjustments in the proof of Lemma 6.2 in [29]. The other two estimates follow by the same adjustments. We first prove

$$ \displaystyle\mu_{q}\left(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t}u^{\ast}H_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})u-t\eta_{\lambda_{1},t}^{-1}\langle\tilde{H}_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})H_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})\rangle\geq\frac{\log N}{N^{1/2}t}\right) \displaystyle\leq e^{-C\log^{2}N}. $$

$$ \displaystyle\mu_{q}\left(-\eta_{\lambda_{1},t}u^{\ast}H_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})u+t\eta_{\lambda_{1},t}^{-1}\langle\tilde{H}_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})H_{\lambda_{1}}(\eta_{\lambda_{1},t})\rangle\geq\frac{\log N}{N^{1/2}t}\right) \displaystyle\leq e^{-C\log^{2}N}. $$

Indeed, to show that the last line holds, we use the inequality $\mathrm{Re}\log[1+ix]\geq Cx^{2}$ for a fixed constant $C>0$ along with ${\operatorname{Tr}\,}H_{\lambda_{j},q_{j}}^{(j-1)}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})^{2}=N\langle H_{\lambda_{j},q_{j}}^{(j-1)}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})^{2}\rangle\gtrsim Nt^{-3}$ . This lets us restrict $\mathrm{d}p$ integration from $\mathbb{R}$ to $|p|\leq N^{\delta}N^{-1/2}t^{3/2}$ . After this, we Taylor expand and control the third-order error term by interlacing $\langle H_{\lambda_{j},q_{j}}^{(j-1)}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})^{k}\rangle=\langle H_{\lambda_{j},q_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})^{k}\rangle+O(N^{-1}t^{-2k})$ and (A1.4) to get $\langle H_{\lambda_{j},q_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})^{k}\rangle\lesssim t^{-2k+2}\langle H_{\lambda_{j},q_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})\rangle\lesssim t^{-2k+1}$ :

$$ \displaystyle{\operatorname{Tr}\,}\log\left[I+ipH_{\lambda_{j},q_{j}}^{(j-1)}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})\right] \displaystyle=iNp\langle H_{\lambda_{j},q_{j}}^{(j-1)}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})\rangle+\frac{1}{2}Np^{2}\langle H_{\lambda_{j},q_{j}}^{(j-1)}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})^{2}\rangle+O(Np^{3}t^{-5})+O(p^{3}t^{-6}) \displaystyle=iNp\langle H_{\lambda_{j},q_{j}}^{(j-1)}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})\rangle+\frac{1}{2}Np^{2}\langle H_{\lambda_{j},q_{j}}^{(j-1)}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})^{2}\rangle+O(N^{3\delta}N^{-1/2}t^{-1/2})+O(N^{3\delta}N^{-3/2}t^{-3/2}). $$

Now use $t\gg N^{-1/2}$ . Finally, by the same token, we can again remove the constraint on $p$ in the $\mathbb{R}$ -integration after controlling the Taylor expansion above. In particular, we have

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{i\frac{N}{t}p}\det[I+ipH_{\lambda_{j},q_{j}}^{(j-1)}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})]^{-1}\mathrm{d}p \displaystyle\approx\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{i\frac{N}{t}p}\exp\left\{-iNp\langle H_{\lambda_{j},q_{j}}^{(j-1)}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})\rangle-\frac{1}{2}Np^{2}\langle H_{\lambda_{j},q_{j}}^{(j-1)}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})^{2}\rangle\right\}\mathrm{d}p \displaystyle=\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{i\frac{N}{t}p[1-t\langle H_{\lambda_{j},q_{j}}^{(j-1)}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})\rangle]}\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2}Np^{2}\langle H_{\lambda_{j},q_{j}}^{(j-1)}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})^{2}\rangle\right\}\mathrm{d}p. $$

By interlacing and Lemma 7, we get $t\langle H_{\lambda_{j},q_{j}}^{(j-1)}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})\rangle=t\langle H_{\lambda_{j},q_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})\rangle+O(N^{-1}t^{-1})=t\langle H_{\lambda_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})\rangle+O(N^{-1}t^{-1})$ . By definition of $\eta_{\lambda_{j},t}$ , we also have $1-t\langle H_{\lambda_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})\rangle=0$ . Hence, for some quantity $\kappa_{N,t,j}=O(N^{-1}t^{-1}))$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{i\frac{N}{t}p[1-t\langle H_{\lambda_{j},q_{j}}^{(j-1)}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})\rangle]}\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2}Np^{2}\langle H_{\lambda_{j},q_{j}}^{(j-1)}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})^{2}\rangle\right\}\mathrm{d}p \displaystyle=\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{i\frac{N}{t}p\kappa_{N,t,j}}\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2}Np^{2}\langle H_{\lambda_{j},q_{j}}^{(j-1)}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})^{2}\rangle\right\}\mathrm{d}p \displaystyle=\frac{\sqrt{2\pi}}{N^{1/2}\langle H_{\lambda_{j},q_{j}}^{(j-1)}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})^{2}\rangle^{1/2}}\exp\left\{-\frac{\kappa_{N,t,j}^{2}}{2N\langle H_{\lambda_{j},q_{j}}^{(j-1)}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})^{2}\rangle}\right\}, $$

where the last line follows by Gaussian integration. Now, we use $\langle H_{\lambda_{j},q_{j}}^{(j-1)}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})^{2}\rangle\lesssim t^{-4}$ , so that

$$ \displaystyle\exp\left\{-\frac{\kappa_{N,t,j}^{2}}{2N\langle H_{\lambda_{j},q_{j}}^{(j-1)}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})^{2}\rangle}\right\} \displaystyle=\exp\left\{O(N^{-3}t^{-6})\right\}\approx 1, $$

where the last bound follows by $t\gg N^{-1/2}$ . On the other hand, by interlacing once again, we have

$$ \displaystyle N^{\frac{1}{2}}\langle H_{\lambda_{j},q_{j}}^{(j-1)}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})^{2}\rangle^{\frac{1}{2}}=N^{\frac{1}{2}}\left\{\langle H_{\lambda_{j},q_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})^{2}\rangle+O(N^{-1}t^{-4})\right\}^{\frac{1}{2}}. $$

By (A1.4), we have $\langle H_{\lambda_{j},q_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})^{2}\rangle\gtrsim t^{-3}$ . Hence, if we now use $t\gg N^{-1}$ , the RHS of the previous display is $\approx N^{1/2}\langle H_{\lambda_{j},q_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})^{2}\rangle^{1/2}$ . At this point, we can follow the display before (4.2) to get

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\sqrt{2\pi}}{N^{1/2}\langle H_{\lambda_{j},q_{j}}^{(j-1)}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})^{2}\rangle^{1/2}}\exp\left\{-\frac{\kappa_{N,t,j}^{2}}{2N\langle H_{\lambda_{j},q_{j}}^{(j-1)}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})^{2}\rangle}\right\}\approx C_{N,t}. $$

By combining our computations thus far, we deduce

$$ \displaystyle K_{j,q_{j},T_{j}} \displaystyle=C_{N,t,j}\det[H_{\lambda_{j},q_{j}}^{(j-1)}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})]\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{i\frac{N}{t}p}\det[I+ipH_{\lambda_{j},q_{j}}^{(j-1)}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})]^{-1}\mathrm{d}p \displaystyle\approx C_{N,t,j}\det[H_{\lambda_{j},q_{j}}^{(j-1)}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})]. $$

By the previous display and elementary resolvent identities (see the display after (6.3) in [29] for the second line below), we have

$$ \displaystyle\det[H_{\lambda_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})]^{-1}K_{j,q_{j},T_{j}}\approx C_{N,t,j}\det[H_{\lambda_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})]^{-1}\det[H_{\lambda_{j},q_{j}}^{(j-1)}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})] \displaystyle\approx C_{N,t,j}\prod_{\ell=1}^{j-1}|\det[V_{\ell}^{\ast}G_{\lambda_{\ell}}^{(\ell-1)}(\eta_{\lambda_{\ell},t})V_{\ell}]|^{-1}\det[H_{\lambda_{j}}^{(j-1)}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})]^{-1}\det[H_{\lambda_{j},q_{j}}^{(j-1)}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})], $$

as well as

$$ \displaystyle\det[H_{\lambda_{j}}^{(j-1)}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})]^{-1}\det[H_{\lambda_{j},q_{j}}^{(j-1)}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})] \displaystyle=\det[I-tq_{j}H_{\lambda_{j}}^{(j-1)}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})T_{j}^{(j-1),\ast}T_{j}^{(j-1)}]^{-1} \displaystyle=\det\left[I-tq_{j}\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\
0&H_{\lambda_{j}}^{(j-1)}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})\end{pmatrix}U_{j-1}^{\ast}T_{j}^{\ast}T_{j}U_{j-1}\right], $$

where the last line follows from recalling that $T_{j}^{(j-1)}$ is the restriction of $T_{j}U_{j-1}$ to the orthogonal complement of $\mathbf{e}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{e}_{j-1}$ . This completes the proof of (5.3). ∎

### 5.2 Proof of (5.4)

By the spectral theorem and finite rank property of $T_{j}$ , we can write $T_{j}^{\ast}T_{j}=\sum_{k=1}^{\ell_{j}}q_{j,k}\mathbf{w}_{j,k}\mathbf{w}_{j,k}^{\ast}$ for $q_{j,k}>0$ . If we define

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{x}_{j,k}^{(j-1)} \displaystyle:=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\
0&H_{\lambda_{j}}^{(j-1)}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})^{\frac{1}{2}}\end{pmatrix}U_{j-1}^{\ast}\mathbf{w}_{j,k}, $$

then we have

$$ \displaystyle\det\left[I-tq_{j}\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\
0&H_{\lambda_{j}}^{(j-1)}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})\end{pmatrix}U_{j-1}^{\ast}T_{j}^{\ast}T_{j}U_{j-1}\right]=\det\left[I-t\sum_{k=1}^{\ell_{j}}q_{j}q_{j,k}\mathbf{x}_{j,k}^{(j-1)}\mathbf{x}_{j,k}^{(j-1),\ast}\right]. $$

Lemma 15 and polarization give $\mathbf{x}_{j,k}^{(j-1),\ast}\mathbf{x}_{j,m}^{(j-1)}=\mathbf{x}_{j,k}^{\ast}\mathbf{x}_{j,m}+\mathcal{O}(N^{-1}t^{-3})$ , where

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{x}_{j,k} \displaystyle:=H_{\lambda_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})^{\frac{1}{2}}\mathbf{w}_{j,k}, $$

We now argue as in the proof of Corollary 3. By (A1.1) and (A3.1), we have $\mathbf{x}_{j,k}^{\ast}\mathbf{x}_{j,m}=O(N^{-1/2}t^{-3/2})$ if $k\neq m$ and $C^{-1}t^{-1}\leq|\mathbf{x}_{j,k}|^{2}\leq Ct^{-1}$ for some $C>0$ . In particular, following the proof of Corollary 3, we have the following on an event $\mathcal{E}$ satisfying $\mathbb{E}_{\bm{\lambda}}\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{E}}=O(N^{-D})$ for any $D>0$ fixed:

$$ \displaystyle\det\left[I-t\sum_{k=1}^{\ell_{j}}q_{j}q_{j,k}\mathbf{x}_{j,k}^{(j-1)}\mathbf{x}_{j,k}^{(j-1),\ast}\right]^{-1} \displaystyle=\prod_{k=1}^{\ell_{j}}\left[1-tq_{j}q_{j,k}|\mathbf{x}_{j,k}^{(j-1)}|^{2}+O(N^{-1}t^{-3})\right]^{-1} \displaystyle\approx\prod_{k=1}^{\ell_{j}}\left[1-tq_{j}q_{j,k}|\mathbf{x}_{j,k}^{(j-1)}|^{2}\right]^{-1} \displaystyle=\prod_{k=1}^{\ell_{j}}\left[1-tq_{j}q_{j,k}\mathbf{w}_{j,k}^{\ast}U_{j-1}\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\
0&H_{\lambda_{j}}^{(j-1)}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})\end{pmatrix}U_{j-1}^{\ast}\mathbf{w}_{j,k}\right]^{-1} \displaystyle=\prod_{k=1}^{\ell_{j}}\left[1-tq_{j}q_{j,k}\mathbf{w}_{j,k}^{\ast}H_{\lambda_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})\mathbf{w}_{j,k}+\mathcal{O}(N^{-1}t^{-3})\right]^{-1}. $$

The second line follows by $tq_{j}q_{j,k}|\mathbf{x}_{j,k}^{(j-1)}|^{2}\gtrsim 1$ that we justified in the previous paragraph and the assumption $t\geq N^{-1/3+\epsilon}$ for some $\epsilon>0$ . The last bound follows again by Lemma 15. Again, we can remove the $\mathcal{O}$ -term by using (A1.1) and (A3.1); this gives $\mathbf{w}_{j,k}^{\ast}H_{\lambda_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})\mathbf{w}_{j,k}=\langle H_{\lambda_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})\rangle[1+O(N^{-1/2}t^{-3/2})]\gtrsim t^{-1}$ . The same reasoning that gave the first line in the above display yields

$$ \displaystyle\prod_{k=1}^{\ell_{j}}\left[1-tq_{j}q_{j,k}\mathbf{w}_{j,k}^{\ast}H_{\lambda_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})\mathbf{w}_{j,k}+\mathcal{O}(N^{-1}t^{-2})\right]^{-1} \displaystyle\approx\det[I-tq_{j}H_{\lambda_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})T_{j}^{\ast}T_{j}]^{-1}, $$

which completes the proof. ∎

## 6 Concentration

In this section we prove the concentration estimates with respect to the measures $\nu_{j}$ and $\omega_{j}$ . First, we state a master concentration inequality below. This was essentially proved in Lemma 6.2 of [29]. We state it in a more general form.

#### Lemma 12 (Master concentration inequality).

For any $j\in\llbracket 1,m_{R}\rrbracket$ and any Hermitian matrix $B\in M_{N-j+1}(\mathbb{C})$ such that

$$ \left\|\sqrt{H^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})}B\sqrt{H^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})}\right\|\leq K\text{ and }{\operatorname{Tr}\,}\left(H^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})B\right)^{2}\leq S, $$

we have

$$ \left|u^{(j-1),\ast}Bu^{(j-1)}-\frac{t}{N}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}H^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})B\right|\prec_{\nu_{j}}\frac{t}{N}\max\left\{\sqrt{S},K\right\}. $$

In particular, in case of rank 1 matrix $B$ , we have

$$ u^{(j-1),\ast}Bu^{(j-1)}\prec_{\nu_{j}}\frac{t}{N}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}H^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})B. $$

For any $j\in\llbracket m_{R}+1,m\rrbracket$ and any Hermitian matrix $B\in M_{N-j+1}(\mathbb{C})$ such that

$$ \left\|\sqrt{\tilde{H}^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})}B\sqrt{\tilde{H}^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})}\right\|\leq K\text{ and }{\operatorname{Tr}\,}\left(\tilde{H}^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})B\right)^{2}\leq S, $$

we have

$$ \left|v^{(j-1),\ast}Bv^{(j-1)}-\frac{t}{N}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}\tilde{H}^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})B\right|\prec_{\nu_{j}}\frac{t}{N}\max\left\{\sqrt{S},K\right\}. $$

In particular, in case of rank 1 matrix $B$ , we have

$$ v^{(j-1),\ast}Bv^{(j-1)}\prec_{\nu_{j}}\frac{t}{N}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}\tilde{H}^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})B. $$

#### Proof.

Consider the right eigenvector case of $j\in\llbracket 1,m_{R}\rrbracket$ . The case of the left eigenvector step $j\in\llbracket m_{R}+1,m\rrbracket$ is proved similarly after replacing $A$ with its adjoint. In the right eigenvector case we show that

$$ \mu\left(u^{(j-1),\ast}Bu^{(j-1)}-\frac{t}{N}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}H^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})B>N^{\delta_{1}}\frac{t}{N}\max\left\{\sqrt{S},KN^{\delta_{1}}\right\}\right)\leq e^{-CN^{\delta_{1}}}. $$

The proof of the other side of the inequality is analogous. Define the moment generating function

$$ m(r,B)=\mathbb{E}_{\mu}\operatorname{exp}\left\{r\left(u^{(j-1),\ast}Bu^{(j-1)}-\frac{t}{N}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}H^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})B\right)\right\}. $$

We take

$$ r=\left(\max\left\{\frac{t\sqrt{S}}{N},\frac{tKN^{\delta_{1}}}{N}\right\}\right)^{-1}=\min\left\{\frac{N}{t\sqrt{S}},\frac{N}{N^{\delta_{1}}tK}\right\}, $$

By Markov’s inequality, we have

$$ \mu\left(r\left(u^{(j-1),\ast}Bu^{(j-1)}-\frac{t}{N}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}H^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})B\right)>N^{\delta_{1}}\right)\leq e^{-N^{\delta_{1}}}m(r,B). $$

In the proof Lemma 6.2 of [29] it is shown that if $\frac{rt}{N}\|B\|<1-c$ for $0<c<1$ , then

$$ m(r,B)\leq\operatorname{exp}\left\{c^{-1}\frac{r^{2}t^{2}}{N^{2}}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}\left(H^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{j}}(\eta_{\lambda_{j},t})B\right)^{2}\right\}. $$

In our case, since $r\leq N^{-\delta_{1}}\frac{N}{tK}$ ,

$$ \frac{rt}{N}\|B\|\leq N^{-\delta_{1}}<1-c. $$

Hence, we have

$$ m(r,B)\leq\operatorname{exp}\left\{c^{-1}\frac{r^{2}t^{2}S}{N^{2}}\right\}\leq\operatorname{exp}\left\{c^{-1}\right\}. $$

Plugging this into (6.5) and dividing by $r$ on the left, we get the desired bound. ∎

#### Lemma 13.

For any $j\in\llbracket 1,m-1\rrbracket$ and $k,l\in\llbracket 1,m\rrbracket$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\left\langle H^{(j)}_{\lambda_{k}}\left(\eta_{\lambda_{k},t}\right)H^{(j)}_{\lambda_{l}}\left(\eta_{\lambda_{l},t}\right)\right\rangle \displaystyle=\left\langle H_{\lambda_{k}}\left(\eta_{\lambda_{k},t}\right)H_{\lambda_{l}}\left(\eta_{\lambda_{l},t}\right)\right\rangle+O\left(\frac{1}{Nt^{4}}\right), \displaystyle\left\langle H^{(j)}_{\lambda_{k}}\left(\eta_{\lambda_{k},t}\right)\tilde{H}^{(j)}_{\lambda_{l}}\left(\eta_{\lambda_{l},t}\right)\right\rangle \displaystyle=\left\langle H_{\lambda_{k}}\left(\eta_{\lambda_{k},t}\right)\tilde{H}_{\lambda_{l}}\left(\eta_{\lambda_{l},t}\right)\right\rangle+O\left(\frac{1}{Nt^{4}}\right), \displaystyle\left\langle\tilde{H}^{(j)}_{\lambda_{k}}\left(\eta_{\lambda_{k},t}\right)\tilde{H}^{(j)}_{\lambda_{l}}\left(\eta_{\lambda_{l},t}\right)\right\rangle \displaystyle=\left\langle\tilde{H}_{\lambda_{k}}\left(\eta_{\lambda_{k},t}\right)\tilde{H}_{\lambda_{l}}\left(\eta_{\lambda_{l},t}\right)\right\rangle+O\left(\frac{1}{Nt^{4}}\right). $$

In particular, these together with A2 imply

$$ \displaystyle\left\langle H^{(j)}_{\lambda_{k}}\left(\eta_{\lambda_{k},t}\right)H^{(j)}_{\lambda_{l}}\left(\eta_{\lambda_{l},t}\right)\right\rangle \displaystyle\gtrsim t^{-2}, \displaystyle\left\langle H^{(j)}_{\lambda_{k}}\left(\eta_{\lambda_{k},t}\right)\tilde{H}^{(j)}_{\lambda_{l}}\left(\eta_{\lambda_{l},t}\right)\right\rangle \displaystyle\gtrsim t^{-1}\left(t+|\lambda_{k}-\lambda_{l}|^{2}\right)^{-1}, \displaystyle\left\langle\tilde{H}^{(j)}_{\lambda_{k}}\left(\eta_{\lambda_{k},t}\right)\tilde{H}^{(j)}_{\lambda_{l}}\left(\eta_{\lambda_{l},t}\right)\right\rangle \displaystyle\gtrsim t^{-2}. $$

#### Proof.

We prove the first estimate, the other two a proved similarly. It is sufficient to show that we can reduce the index $j$ by $1$ with the error $O\left(\frac{1}{Nt^{4}}\right)$ , i.e.

$$ \left\langle H^{(j)}_{\lambda_{k}}\left(\eta_{\lambda_{k},t}\right)H^{(j)}_{\lambda_{l}}\left(\eta_{\lambda_{l},t}\right)\right\rangle=\left\langle H^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{k}}\left(\eta_{\lambda_{k},t}\right)H^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{l}}\left(\eta_{\lambda_{l},t}\right)\right\rangle+O\left(\frac{1}{Nt^{4}}\right). $$

We will consider $j\in\llbracket 1,m_{R}\rrbracket$ , the other case is proved the same way, the only modification is the replacement of $u^{(j-1)}$ with $v^{(j-1)}$ . For $i=k,l$ consider

$$ \hat{H}^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{i}}(\eta_{\lambda_{i},t})=\left[\left(A^{(j-1)}-\lambda_{i}\right)^{\ast}(I-u^{(j-1)}u^{(j-1),\ast})\left(A^{(j-1)}-\lambda_{i}\right)+\eta_{\lambda_{i},t}^{2}\right]^{-1}. $$

By Lemma 2.1 of [29], we have

$$ \displaystyle\left\langle H^{(j)}_{\lambda_{k}}\left(\eta_{\lambda_{k},t}\right)H^{(j)}_{\lambda_{l}}\left(\eta_{\lambda_{l},t}\right)\right\rangle \displaystyle=\left\langle\hat{H}^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{k}}\left(\eta_{\lambda_{k},t}\right)\hat{H}^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{l}}\left(\eta_{\lambda_{l},t}\right)\right\rangle \displaystyle-\frac{u^{(j-1),\ast}\hat{H}^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{k}}(\eta_{\lambda_{k},t})\hat{H}^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{l}}(\eta_{\lambda_{l},t})\hat{H}^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{k}}(\eta_{\lambda_{k},t})u^{(j-1)}}{Nu^{(j-1),\ast}\hat{H}^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{k}}(\eta_{\lambda_{k},t})u^{(j-1)}} \displaystyle-\frac{u^{(j-1),\ast}\hat{H}^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{l}}(\eta_{\lambda_{l},t})\hat{H}^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{k}}(\eta_{\lambda_{k},t})\hat{H}^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{l}}(\eta_{\lambda_{l},t})u^{(j-1)}}{Nu^{(j-1),\ast}\hat{H}^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{l}}(\eta_{\lambda_{l},t})u^{(j-1)}} \displaystyle+\frac{\left|u^{(j-1),\ast}\hat{H}^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{k}}(\eta_{\lambda_{k},t})\hat{H}^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{l}}(\eta_{\lambda_{l},t})u^{(j-1)}\right|^{2}}{Nu^{(j-1),\ast}\hat{H}^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{k}}(\eta_{\lambda_{k},t})u^{(j-1)}u^{(j-1),\ast}\hat{H}^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{l}}(\eta_{\lambda_{l},t})u^{(j-1)}}. $$

To bound the second and the third term we note that

$$ u^{(j-1),\ast}\hat{H}^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{k}}(\eta_{\lambda_{k},t})\hat{H}^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{l}}(\eta_{\lambda_{l},t})\hat{H}^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{k}}(\eta_{\lambda_{k},t})u^{(j-1)}\lesssim t^{-4}u^{(j-1),\ast}\hat{H}^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{k}}(\eta_{\lambda_{k},t})u^{(j-1)} $$

and to bound the last term we note that

$$ \displaystyle\left|u^{(j-1),\ast}\hat{H}^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{k}}(\eta_{\lambda_{k},t})\hat{H}^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{l}}(\eta_{\lambda_{l},t})u^{(j-1)}\right|^{2}\leq\left\|\hat{H}^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{k}}(\eta_{\lambda_{k},t})u^{(j-1)}\right\|^{2}\left\|\hat{H}^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{l}}(\eta_{\lambda_{l},t})u^{(j-1)}\right\|^{2} \displaystyle\lesssim t^{-4}u^{(j-1),\ast}\hat{H}^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{k}}(\eta_{\lambda_{k},t})u^{(j-1)}u^{(j-1),\ast}\hat{H}^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{l}}(\eta_{\lambda_{l},t})u^{(j-1)}. $$

Then

$$ \displaystyle\left\langle H^{(j)}_{\lambda_{k}}\left(\eta_{\lambda_{k},t}\right)H^{(j)}_{\lambda_{l}}\left(\eta_{\lambda_{l},t}\right)\right\rangle \displaystyle=\left\langle\hat{H}^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{k}}\left(\eta_{\lambda_{k},t}\right)\hat{H}^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{l}}\left(\eta_{\lambda_{l},t}\right)\right\rangle+O\left(\frac{1}{Nt^{4}}\right) $$

Now we use Woodbury’s identity to get

$$ \displaystyle\left\langle\hat{H}^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{k}}\left(\eta_{\lambda_{k},t}\right)\hat{H}^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{l}}\left(\eta_{\lambda_{l},t}\right)\right\rangle=\left\langle H^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{k}}\left(\eta_{\lambda_{k},t}\right)H^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{l}}\left(\eta_{\lambda_{l},t}\right)\right\rangle \displaystyle+\frac{u^{(j-1),\ast}(A^{(j-1)}-\lambda_{k})H^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{k}}(\eta_{\lambda_{k},t})H^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{l}}(\eta_{\lambda_{l},t})H^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{k}}(\eta_{\lambda_{k},t})(A^{(j-1)}-\lambda_{k})^{\ast}u^{(j-1)}}{N\eta_{\lambda_{k},t}^{2}u^{(j-1),\ast}\tilde{H}^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{k}}\left(\eta_{\lambda_{k},t}\right)u^{(j-1)}} \displaystyle+\frac{u^{(j-1),\ast}(A^{(j-1)}-\lambda_{l})H^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{l}}(\eta_{\lambda_{l},t})H^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{k}}(\eta_{\lambda_{k},t})H^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{l}}(\eta_{\lambda_{l},t})(A^{(j-1)}-\lambda_{l})^{\ast}u^{(j-1)}}{N\eta_{\lambda_{l},t}^{2}u^{(j-1),\ast}\tilde{H}^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{l}}\left(\eta_{\lambda_{l},t}\right)u^{(j-1)}} \displaystyle+\frac{\left|u^{(j-1),\ast}(A^{(j-1)}-\lambda_{k})H^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{k}}(\eta_{\lambda_{k},t})H^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{l}}(\eta_{\lambda_{l},t})(A^{(j-1)}-\lambda_{l})^{\ast}u^{(j-1)}\right|^{2}}{N\eta_{\lambda_{k},t}^{2}\eta_{\lambda_{l},t}^{2}u^{(j-1),\ast}\tilde{H}^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{k}}\left(\eta_{\lambda_{k},t}\right)u^{(j-1)}u^{(j-1),\ast}\tilde{H}^{(j-1)}_{\lambda_{l}}\left(\eta_{\lambda_{l},t}\right)u^{(j-1)}}. $$

To bound the first two error terms we note that

0,&x\leq 1.1\end{cases} $$

For convenience, set $B:=B_{z_{0}}(RN^{-1/2})$ . We claim that for some $c>0$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\phi\left(\max_{z\in B}\frac{\eta}{2}\mathrm{Im}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}G_{z}(\eta)\right)\right]\leq N^{-c}, $$

where the expectation is over randomness of the matrix $A$ . To see that this is enough, we first note

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\eta}{2}\mathrm{Im}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}G_{z}(\eta) \displaystyle=\sum_{k=1}^{N}\frac{\eta^{2}}{(\xi_{k}^{z})^{2}+\eta^{2}}\geq\frac{2\eta^{2}}{(\xi_{2}^{z})^{2}+\eta^{2}}+\sum_{k=3}^{N}\frac{\eta^{2}}{(\xi_{k}^{z})^{2}+\eta^{2}}. $$

Thus, if there is $z\in B$ for which $\xi_{2}^{z}\leq N^{-1-\delta}\ll\eta$ , then on this event, we have

$$ \displaystyle\eta\mathrm{Im}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}G_{z}(\eta)\geq 2\frac{\eta^{2}}{(\xi_{2}^{z})^{2}+\eta^{2}}\geq 1.9. $$

In particular, since this statement is deterministic in $z$ , we have the bounds

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(\exists\lambda\in\mathrm{Spec}(A)\cap B_{z_{0}}(RN^{-1/2}):\ \xi_{2}^{\lambda}\leq N^{-1-\delta}\right) \displaystyle\leq\mathbb{P}\left(\max_{z\in B}\frac{\eta}{2}\mathrm{Im}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}G_{z}(\eta)\geq 1.9\right) \displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}\left[\phi\left(\max_{z\in B}\frac{\eta}{2}\mathrm{Im}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}G_{z}(\eta)\right)\right], $$

at which point we conclude. To prove the remaining estimate (7.8), Let $\mathcal{E}\subseteq B$ be such that the distance between any point in $B$ to $\mathcal{E}$ is at most $N^{1/2-\epsilon}\eta$ , and $|\mathcal{E}|=O(N^{2\epsilon+2\delta_{1}})$ . $$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\phi\left(\max_{z\in B\cap\mathcal{E}}\frac{\eta}{2}\mathrm{Im}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}G_{z}(\eta)\right)\right] \displaystyle\leq\sum_{z\in B\cap\mathcal{E}}\mathbb{P}\left(\frac{\eta}{2}\mathrm{Im}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}G_{z}(\eta)\geq 1.1\right) \displaystyle\leq\sum_{z\in B\cap\mathcal{E}}\mathbb{P}\left(\xi_{2}^{z}\leq N^{-1-\delta_{2}}\right) \displaystyle\leq|\mathcal{E}|N^{-2.1\delta_{2}}\lesssim N^{2\epsilon+2\delta_{1}-2.1\delta_{2}}. $$

The first bound follows by union bound and definition of $\phi$ . To show the second bound, we first use the identity in (7.9) to get the upper bound

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\eta}{2}\mathrm{Im}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}G_{z}(\eta) \displaystyle\leq 1+\sum_{k=2}^{N}\frac{\eta^{2}}{(\xi_{k}^{z})^{2}+\eta^{2}}. $$

If the LHS of the previous display is $\geq 1.1$ , then $\xi_{2}^{z}\leq N^{-1-\delta_{2}}$ (for $N$ large enough). Indeed, if not, then the $k=2$ term in the sum is $O(N^{-\kappa})$ . The same is true for the first $N^{\tau}$ many terms, where $\tau<\kappa$ . Now we use rigidity to handle the remaining terms; see the proof of Lemma 21, for example. The last line follows by Proposition 23. By construction of $\delta_{2}$ , we deduce

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\phi\left(\max_{z\in B\cap\mathcal{E}}\frac{\eta}{2}\mathrm{Im}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}G_{z}(\eta)\right)\right]\leq N^{-c}. $$

To extend from $B\cap\mathcal{E}$ to $B$ , take any $z_{1}\in B$ and $z_{2}\in\mathcal{E}$ . By (7.2) for $T=I$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle|\eta{\operatorname{Tr}\,}G_{z_{1}}(\eta)-\eta{\operatorname{Tr}\,}G_{z_{2}}(\eta)| \displaystyle=\mathcal{O}(N^{-1/2}\eta^{-1}|z_{1}-z_{2}|). $$

Now use $|z_{1}-z_{2}|\leq N^{1/2-\epsilon}\eta$ to conclude. ∎

and $m_{z}(i\eta)$ is defined via the self-consistent equation

where we recall $\eta_{V}=N^{-1-\delta_{V}}$ with $\delta_{V}>0$ small. Next, by (3.2) in [13], which is a deterministic identity that holds even for our random test function $f^{(j)}$ in place of $g$ therein, we must first prove the following estimates:

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{C}}\Delta f^{(j)}(z)\log|\det[\mathcal{H}_{z}-iT]|\mathrm{d}^{2}z \displaystyle=\mathcal{O}(N^{-98}\|\Delta\tilde{f}^{(j)}\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{C})})=\mathcal{O}(N^{-94}), \displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{C}}\Delta f^{(j)}(z)\int_{N^{100}}^{+\infty}\left(\mathrm{Im}m_{z}(i\eta)-\frac{1}{\eta+1}\right)\mathrm{d}\eta\mathrm{d}^{2}z \displaystyle=\mathcal{O}(N^{-98}\|\Delta\tilde{f}^{(j)}\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{C})})=\mathcal{O}(N^{-94}), $$

$$ \displaystyle I_{0}^{\eta_{0}} \displaystyle:=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb{C}}\Delta f^{(j)}(z)\int_{0}^{\eta_{0}}\langle\mathrm{Im}G_{z}(\eta)-\mathrm{Im}m_{z}(i\eta)\rangle\mathrm{d}\eta\mathrm{d}^{2}z, \displaystyle I_{\eta_{1}}^{N^{100}} \displaystyle:=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb{C}}\Delta f^{(j)}(z)\int_{\eta_{1}}^{N^{100}}\langle\mathrm{Im}G_{z}(\eta)-\mathrm{Im}m_{z}(i\eta)\rangle\mathrm{d}\eta\mathrm{d}^{2}z, $$

$$ \displaystyle I_{0}^{\eta_{0}} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb{C}}\Delta f^{(j)}(z)\times\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\lambda_{k}<N^{-L}}\log\left(1+\frac{\eta_{0}^{2}}{\lambda_{k}^{2}}\right)\mathrm{d}^{2}z \displaystyle+\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb{C}}\Delta f^{(j)}(z)\times\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\lambda_{k}\geq N^{-L}}\log\left(1+\frac{\eta_{0}^{2}}{\lambda_{k}^{2}}\right)\mathrm{d}^{2}z \displaystyle-\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb{C}}\Delta f^{(j)}(z)\times\int_{0}^{\eta_{0}}\mathrm{Im}m_{z}(i\eta)\mathrm{d}^{2}z \displaystyle=\mathrm{I}+\mathrm{II}+\mathrm{III}. $$

$$ \displaystyle I_{\delta_{V}}(\tilde{M}_{t},f^{(j)}):=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb{C}}\Delta f^{(j)}(z)\int_{N^{-1-10\delta_{V}}}^{N^{-1+10\delta_{V}}}\langle\mathrm{Im}G_{z,t}(\eta)-\mathrm{Im}m_{z}(i\eta)\rangle\mathrm{d}\eta\mathrm{d}^{2}z, $$

where $G_{z,t}$ is $G_{z}$ but with $\tilde{M}_{t}$ instead of $A$ . Precisely, by the proof of Proposition 2.5 in [13], we have the following.

### 7.2 Proof of (7.10)

#### Definition 27.

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{H}^{0}:=\tilde{\mathcal{H}}=\begin{pmatrix}0&\tilde{M}_{t}\\
\tilde{M}_{t}^{\ast}&0\end{pmatrix},\quad\mathcal{H}^{1}:=\mathcal{H}=\begin{pmatrix}0&A\\

First, the triple $(\mathcal{H}^{0},\mathcal{H}^{\theta},\mathcal{H}^{1})$ is jointly independent. Second, the marginal distribution of $\mathcal{H}^{\theta}$ is given by the product measure

$$ \displaystyle\prod_{i,j}\rho_{ij}^{\theta}(\mathrm{d}\mathcal{H}_{ij}^{\theta}). $$

$$ \displaystyle(\mathcal{H}^{\theta,\lambda}_{(ij)})_{k\ell}:=\begin{cases}\mathcal{H}_{(ij)}^{\theta}&(i,j)\neq(k,\ell)\\
\lambda&(i,j)=(k,\ell)\end{cases} $$

$$ \displaystyle G_{z}^{\theta}(\eta):=\left[\mathcal{H}^{\theta}-\begin{pmatrix}0&z\\

Now, by the Leibniz rule, to show (7.12)-(7.13) with the above choice of $F$ , it suffices to show that for any $n\geq 0$ and locally uniformly in $w_{j}\in\mathbb{C}$ and $\eta_{j}\in\mathcal{I}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\mathcal{H}^{\theta}_{ij}}\right)^{n}\mathcal{A}_{j}(\mathcal{H}^{\theta},w_{j},\eta_{j})=\mathcal{O}\left(N^{C_{n}\delta_{V}}\right), $$

where $\mathcal{A}_{j}(\mathcal{H}^{\theta},w_{j},\eta_{j})$ either has the form $g(V(z_{j}^{0}+N^{-1/2}w_{j},T))$ with $T$ finite-rank and Hermitian and $g\in C^{\infty}_{c}(\mathbb{C})$ or the form $\langle\mathrm{Im}G_{z_{j}^{0}+N^{-1/2}w_{j}}^{\theta}(\eta_{j})-\mathrm{Im}m_{z_{j}^{0}+N^{-1/2}w_{j}}(i\eta_{j})\rangle$ . (Such $\mathcal{A}_{j}(\mathcal{H}^{\theta},w_{j},\eta_{j})$ have $m$ -th order derivatives that are deterministically $O(N^{C_{m}})$ if $\eta_{j}\geq N^{-1-10\delta_{V}}$ and $\delta_{V}>0$ is small; this can be checked by elementary resolvent perturbation identities. Thus, an $\mathcal{O}$ -estimate is enough. We also note that straightforward regularity bounds in $\theta$ of $\mathcal{A}_{j}(\mathcal{H}^{\theta},w_{j},\eta_{j})$ let us use a net argument to extend (7.14) to the same estimate but with a supremum over $\theta\in[0,1]$ , upon possibly changing the constant $C_{n}>0$ .)

We are left to prove (7.14). First, the assumption $g\in C^{\infty}_{c}(\mathbb{C})$ and the local law (see Theorem 2.6 in [12]) imply (7.14) for $n=0$ , so we focus on $n\geq 1$ . By definition of $V(z,T)$ , it suffices to show that locally uniformly in $z\in\mathbb{C}$ and uniformly in $\eta\in[N^{-1-10\delta_{V}},N^{-1+10\delta_{V}}]$ , for any finite-rank, Hermitian $T$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\mathcal{H}^{\theta}_{ij}}\right)^{n}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}TG^{\theta}_{z}(\eta) \displaystyle=\mathcal{O}(N^{C_{n}\delta_{V}}) \displaystyle\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\mathcal{H}^{\theta}_{ij}}\right)^{n}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}\mathrm{Im}G^{\theta}_{z}(\eta) \displaystyle=\mathcal{O}(N^{1+C_{n}\delta_{V}}). $$

For this, we record the following consequence of resolvent perturbation identities:

$$ \displaystyle\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\mathcal{H}^{\theta}_{ij}}\right)^{n}G_{z}^{\theta}(\eta) \displaystyle=C_{n}G_{z}^{\theta}(\eta)\left[\Delta_{ij}G_{z}^{\theta}(\eta)\right]^{n},\quad(\Delta_{ij})_{k\ell}=\delta_{ik}\delta_{\ell j}+\delta_{i\ell}\delta_{jk}. $$

Using this identity and a spectral decomposition $T=\sum_{a=1}^{\ell}\tau_{a}\mathbf{w}_{a}\mathbf{w}_{a}^{\ast}$ we have

$$ \displaystyle\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\mathcal{H}^{\theta}_{ij}}\right)^{n}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}TG_{z}^{\eta}(\eta) \displaystyle=C_{n}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}TG_{z}^{\theta}(\eta)[\Delta_{ij}G_{z}^{\theta}(\eta)]^{n}G_{z}^{\theta}(\eta) \displaystyle=\sum_{a=1}^{\ell}C_{n}\tau_{a}\mathbf{w}_{a}^{\ast}G_{z}^{\theta}(\eta)\mathbf{e}_{i}\mathbf{e}_{j}^{\ast}G_{z}^{\theta}(\eta)\mathbf{e}_{i}\ldots\mathbf{e}_{j}^{\ast}G_{z}^{\theta}(\eta)\mathbf{w}_{a}, $$

where the product has at most $n+2$ many factors of the form $\mathbf{x}^{\ast}G_{z}^{\theta}(\eta)\mathbf{y}$ with $\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}$ deterministic unit vectors. By rigidity and delocalization, i.e. Proposition 30, for eigenvalues $\xi_{k}$ and eigenvectors $\mathbf{u}_{k}$ of $G_{z}^{\theta}(\eta)$ , we have the following for some $c>0$ independent of $N$ :

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{x}^{\ast}G_{z}^{\theta}(\eta)\mathbf{y} \displaystyle=\sum_{k}\frac{\mathbf{x}^{\ast}\mathbf{u}_{k}\mathbf{u}_{k}^{\ast}\mathbf{y}}{\xi_{k}-i\eta}=\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k}\frac{1}{\xi_{k}-i\eta}\right)+\sum_{k:|\xi_{k}|\geq c}\frac{\mathbf{x}^{\ast}\mathbf{u}_{k}\mathbf{u}_{k}^{\ast}\mathbf{y}}{\xi_{k}-i\eta} \displaystyle=\mathcal{O}(N^{-1}\eta^{-1})+O(1)=\mathcal{O}(N^{10\delta_{V}}). $$

The last term in the first line has the form $\mathbf{x}^{\ast}Y\mathbf{y}$ , where $\|Y\|_{\mathrm{op}}=O(1)$ , hence it is $O(1)$ .

Combining the previous two displays gives (7.15). To prove (7.16), we write $\mathrm{Im}G_{z}^{\theta}(\eta)=G_{z}^{\theta}(\eta)-G_{z}^{\theta}(\eta)^{\ast}$ . In particular, it suffices to prove (7.16) but with $\mathrm{Im}G_{z}^{\theta}(\eta)$ replaced by $G_{z}^{\theta}(\eta)$ and $G_{z}^{\theta}(\eta)^{\ast}$ . We prove (7.16) with $\mathrm{Im}G_{z}^{\theta}(\eta)$ replaced by $G_{z}^{\theta}(\eta)$ ; for $G_{z}^{\theta}(\eta)^{\ast}$ , the same argument works. Note that

$$ \displaystyle\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\mathcal{H}^{\theta}_{ij}}\right)^{n}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}G^{\theta}_{z}(\eta) \displaystyle=\sum_{k=1}^{2N}\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\mathcal{H}^{\theta}_{ij}}\right)^{n}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}\mathbf{e}_{k}\mathbf{e}_{k}^{\ast}G^{\theta}_{z}(\eta). $$

The estimate (7.15) with $T=\mathbf{e}_{k}\mathbf{e}_{k}^{\ast}$ implies that the RHS of the previous display is $\mathcal{O}(N^{1+C_{n}\delta_{V}})$ . This proves (7.16), so as mentioned right before (7.15), this shows (7.14) and thus completes the proof of Theorem 1. ∎

### 7.3 Proof of Proposition 23

This argument has three steps. First, we reduce to proving the estimate for $\xi_{2}^{z}(t)$ , the second-smallest singular value of the matching matrix $\tilde{M}_{t}$ from Lemma 18. Then, we further reduce to proving the estimate for the second-smallest singular value of a Ginibre matrix. Finally, we cite known estimates for the Ginibre case. As argued in the proof of Lemma 24, we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\xi_{2}^{z}\leq N^{-1-\delta})\lesssim\mathbb{E}\left[\phi\left(\frac{\eta}{2}\mathrm{Im}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}G_{z}(\eta)\right)\right]. $$

Now, define $G_{t,z}(\eta):=[\mathcal{H}_{t,z}-i\eta]^{-1}$ , where $\mathcal{H}_{t,z}$ is defined by

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{t,z} \displaystyle:=\begin{pmatrix}0&\tilde{M}_{t}-z\\
(\tilde{M}_{t}-z)^{\ast}&0\end{pmatrix}. $$

Since $\phi:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is smooth and compactly supported, we can use (7.16) and $\eta\leq N^{-1}$ and Lemma 28 to deduce

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\phi\left(\frac{\eta}{2}\mathrm{Im}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}G_{z}(\eta)\right)\right]-\mathbb{E}\left[\phi\left(\frac{\eta}{2}\mathrm{Im}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}G_{t,z}(\eta)\right)\right]=O(N^{-\delta_{t}/2}). $$

(The input (7.13) to use Lemma 28 can be shown, again, by (7.16) and a standard net argument.) As argued in the proof of Lemma 24, we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\phi\left(\frac{\eta}{2}\mathrm{Im}{\operatorname{Tr}\,}G_{t,z}(\eta)\right)\right]\lesssim\mathbb{P}(\xi_{2}^{z}(t)\leq N^{-1-\delta_{2}}), $$

where $\xi_{2}^{z}(t)$ is the second-smallest (positive) singular value of $\tilde{M}_{t}$ , and $\delta_{2}$ is any fixed number strictly smaller than $\delta_{1}$ . Summarizing so far, we have proven

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\xi_{2}^{z}\leq N^{-1-\delta})\lesssim\mathbb{P}(\xi_{2}^{z}(t)\leq N^{-1-\delta_{2}})+N^{-\delta_{t}/2}. $$

We now use Theorem 3.2 in [11]. This gives the following. There exists a matrix $W(t)$ whose entries are i.i.d. standard complex Gaussians mutiplied by $(1+t)^{1/2}$ such that if $\{\mu_{k}(t)\}_{k}$ are the singular values of $W(t)$ with $\mu_{k}(t)\leq\mu_{k+1}(t)$ for $k\geq 1$ and $\mu_{-k}(t)=\mu_{k}(t)$ , then

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(|\xi_{2}^{z}(t)-\mu_{2}^{z}(t)|\leq N^{-1-\kappa}\right)\lesssim N^{-D} $$

for any fixed $D>0$ , where $\kappa>0$ is fixed. (This requires that $\langle\mathrm{Im}G_{t,z}(\eta)\rangle=\mathcal{O}(1)$ for all $\eta\geq N^{-1+\epsilon}$ for some $\epsilon>0$ fixed. Such an estimate follows by the local law in (3.6) in [17] combined with (3.7) in [17].) Since $\kappa>0$ is fixed, for small enough $\delta$ , we deduce

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\xi_{2}^{z}\leq N^{-1-\delta})\lesssim\mathbb{P}(\mu_{2}(t)\leq N^{-1-\delta_{2}})+N^{-\delta_{t}/2}=\mathbb{P}((1+t)^{1/2}\mu_{2}(0)\leq N^{-1-\delta_{2}})+N^{-\delta_{t}/2}. $$

We now use Theorem 2.10 in [19]; this shows that the first term on the far RHS of the previous display is $O(N^{\epsilon}N^{-8\delta_{2}})$ with $\epsilon>0$ fixed but otherwise arbitrary. If we choose $\epsilon>0$ small enough and $\delta_{2}$ sufficiently close to $\delta_{1}$ , then the far RHS of the previous display becomes $O(N^{-2.1\delta})$ for $\delta>0$ small enough. This completes the proof.

## 8 Green’s function estimates

The purpose of this section is to record various auxiliary bounds for Green’s functions. These bounds are mostly standard. First, recall the Hermitization $\mathcal{H}_{z}$ of $A$ and Green’s function:

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{z}:=\begin{pmatrix}0&A-z\\
(A-z)^{\ast}&0\end{pmatrix}\quad\mathrm{and}\quad G_{z}(\eta):=[\mathcal{H}_{z}-i\eta]^{-1} $$

for $\eta>0$ . Green’s function can be written as

$$ G_{z}(\eta)=\begin{pmatrix}i\eta\tilde{H}_{z}(\eta)&\tilde{H}_{z}(\eta)(A-z)\\
(A^{\ast}-\bar{z})\tilde{H}_{z}(\eta)&i\eta H_{z}(\eta)\end{pmatrix}, $$

where

$$ \displaystyle H_{z}(\eta) \displaystyle=\left[(A-z)^{\ast}(A-z)+\eta^{2}\right]^{-1}, \displaystyle\tilde{H}_{z}(\eta) \displaystyle=\left[(A-z)(A-z)^{\ast}+\eta^{2}\right]^{-1}. $$

We assume $A$ has entries that satisfy $\mathbb{E}A_{ij}=0$ and $\mathbb{E}A_{ij}^{2}=N^{-1}$ and $\mathbb{E}|A_{ij}|^{p}\leq C_{p}N^{-p/2}$ for all $p\geq 2$ . As in Definition 20, we let $\xi_{k}^{z}$ be eigenvalues of the Hermitization $\mathcal{H}_{z}$ , and we let $\mathbf{u}_{k}^{z}$ be the corresponding eigenvalues. We adopt the convention $\xi_{k}^{z}\geq 0$ for all $k\in\llbracket 1,N\rrbracket$ , and $\xi_{k}^{z}=-\xi_{-k}^{z}$ for any $k\in\llbracket-N,-1\rrbracket$ . We also impose $\xi_{k}^{z}\leq\xi_{\ell}^{z}$ for $k\leq\ell$ .

We now introduce a deterministic local law approximation for $G_{z}$ . Define

$$ \displaystyle M_{z}(w):=\begin{pmatrix}m_{z}(w)&-zu_{z}(w)\\
-\overline{z}u_{z}(w)&m_{z}(w)\end{pmatrix},\quad u_{z}(w):=\frac{m_{z}(w)}{w+m_{z}(w)}, $$

where $m_{z}(w)$ satisfies the self-consistent equation

$$ \displaystyle-\frac{1}{m_{z}(w)}=w+m_{z}(w)-\frac{|z|^{2}}{w+m_{z}(w)},\quad\mathrm{Im}[m_{z}(w)]\mathrm{Im}[w]>0. $$

#### Proposition 29.

Fix any deterministic matrix $Y\in M_{2N}(\mathbb{C})$ with $\|Y\|_{\mathrm{op}}=O(1)$ and any deterministic unit vectors $\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{C}^{2N}$ . Fix any $\tau>0$ . Fix any $\eta\geq N^{-1+\epsilon}$ for any $\epsilon>0$ , and fix $|z|\leq 1-\tau$ . We have

$$ \displaystyle\langle Y(G_{z}(\eta)-M_{z}(i\eta))\rangle \displaystyle=\mathcal{O}\left(N^{-1}\eta^{-1}\right) \displaystyle\mathbf{x}^{\ast}(G_{z}(\eta)-M_{z}(i\eta))\mathbf{y} \displaystyle=\mathcal{O}\left(N^{-1/2}\eta^{-1/2}\right). $$

In particular, we have (A3.1)-(A3.2).

#### Proof.

The first two bounds are (3.6) in [17]. We now show (A3.1); the proof of (A3.2) is similar. We use the first two bounds with $Y=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\ 0&I_{N}\end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{x}^{\ast}=\begin{pmatrix}0&\mathbf{w}_{1}^{\ast}\end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{y}^{\ast}=\begin{pmatrix}0&\mathbf{w}_{2}^{\ast}\end{pmatrix}$ , so

$$ \displaystyle i\eta\mathbf{w}_{1}^{\ast}H_{z}(\eta)\mathbf{w}_{2}-m_{z}(i\eta)\mathbf{w}_{1}^{\ast}\mathbf{w}_{2} \displaystyle=\mathcal{O}(N^{-1/2}\eta^{-1/2}) \displaystyle\langle i\eta H_{z}(\eta)\rangle-m_{z}(i\eta) \displaystyle=\mathcal{O}(N^{-1}\eta^{-1}). $$

This gives (A3.1). ∎

Define the following limiting empirical spectral density of $\mathcal{H}_{z}$ for $E\in\mathbb{R}$ :

$$ \displaystyle\rho_{z}(E):=\lim_{\eta\to 0^{+}}\frac{1}{\pi}|\mathrm{Im}m_{z}(E+i\eta)|. $$

With this, we define two objects. The first is the quantile $\gamma_{j,z}$ for any $|j|\leq N$ via the equation

$$ \displaystyle\frac{j+N}{2N}=\int_{-\infty}^{\gamma_{j,z}}\rho_{z}(E)\mathrm{d}E. $$

Note that $\gamma_{j,z}=-\gamma_{-j,z}$ . The second is the $\kappa$ -bulk $\mathbb{B}_{\kappa,z}:=\{E\in\mathbb{R}:\rho_{z}(E)\geq\kappa^{1/3}\}$ , where $\kappa>0$ . These notations are taken from Section 2 of [12]. By Example 2.5 in [12], if $|z|\leq 1-\tau$ with $\tau>0$ fixed, then we can take $\kappa>0$ small enough depending only on $\tau$ such that $\mathbb{B}_{\kappa,z}$ contains an interval around $0$ .

#### Proposition 30 (Rigidity and delocalization, Corollaries 2.8 and 2.9 in [2]).

Suppose $|z|\leq 1-\tau$ for some $\tau>0$ . Fix any $\kappa>0$ small enough, and suppose $\gamma_{k,z}\in\mathbb{B}_{\kappa,z}$ . We have $|\xi_{k}^{z}-\gamma_{k,z}|=\mathcal{O}(N^{-1})$ . Moreover, we have $\|\mathbf{u}_{k}^{z}\|_{\infty}=\mathcal{O}(N^{-1/2})$ .

Next, we note that

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{Im}[M_{z}(E)] \displaystyle=\mathrm{Im}[m_{z}(E)]-\frac{E+o(E)}{\mathrm{Im}[m_{z}(0)]}\begin{pmatrix}0&-z\\
-\overline{z}&0\end{pmatrix},\quad\mathrm{Im}[m_{z}(0)]=\sqrt{1-|z|^{2}}. $$

#### Proposition 31 (Eigenstate thermalization hypothesis, Theorem 2.7 in [12]).

Fix any deterministic matrix $Y\in M_{2N}(\mathbb{C})$ such that $\|Y\|_{\mathrm{op}}=O(1)$ . We have

$$ \displaystyle\max_{|i|,|j|\leq N}\left|\mathbf{u}_{i}^{z,\ast}Y\mathbf{u}_{j}^{z}-\delta_{ij}\frac{\langle\mathrm{Im}M_{z}(\gamma_{j})Y\rangle}{\langle\mathrm{Im}M_{z}(\gamma_{j})\rangle}-\delta_{-ij}\frac{\langle\mathrm{Im}M_{z}(\gamma_{j})(E_{11}-E_{22})Y\rangle}{\langle\mathrm{Im}M_{z}(\gamma_{j})\rangle}\right|=\mathcal{O}(N^{-\frac{1}{2}}), $$

where $\mathcal{O}$ is with respect to randomness of $A$ , while $E_{11},E_{22}$ are the $2N\times 2N$ block matrices

$$ \displaystyle E_{11}:=\begin{pmatrix}I_{N}&0\\
0&0\end{pmatrix}\quad\mathrm{and}\quad E_{22}:=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\
0&I_{N}\end{pmatrix}. $$

Thus, by (8.2), if $\langle YE_{11}\rangle,\langle YE_{22}\rangle=0$ , then

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{u}_{i}^{z,\ast}Y\mathbf{u}_{j}^{z}=\delta_{|i|=|j|}O(N^{-1}i)+\mathcal{O}(N^{-1/2}). $$

#### Proposition 32.

Suppose $|z_{1}|,|z_{2}|\leq 1-\tau$ for some $\tau>0$ and $\eta_{1},\eta_{2}\in[N^{-\frac{1}{3}+\epsilon_{0}},10]$ . Define $\eta^{\ast}=\max\{\eta_{1},\eta_{2}\}$ . Then there exists a constant $c>0$ such that for any $D>0$ we have

$$ \displaystyle{\mathbb{P}}\left(\left\langle H_{z_{1}}(\eta_{1})H_{z_{2}}(\eta_{2})\right\rangle\leq c\left(\eta^{\ast}\right)^{-2}\right)\leq N^{-D} \displaystyle{\mathbb{P}}\left(\left\langle\tilde{H}_{z_{1}}(\eta_{1})\tilde{H}_{z_{2}}(\eta_{2})\right\rangle\leq c\left(\eta^{\ast}\right)^{-2}\right)\leq N^{-D} \displaystyle{\mathbb{P}}\left(\left\langle H_{z_{1}}(\eta_{1})\tilde{H}_{z_{2}}(\eta_{2})\right\rangle\leq\frac{c}{\eta^{\ast}\left(\eta^{\ast}+|z_{1}-z_{2}|^{2}\right)}\right)\leq N^{-D} $$

for large enough $N$ uniformly in $z_{1},z_{2},\eta_{1},\eta_{2}$ .

#### Proof.

Define $\eta_{\ast}=\min\{\eta_{1},\eta_{2}\}$ . To show (8.3), we note that

$$ \left\langle H_{z_{1}}(\eta_{1})H_{z_{2}}(\eta_{2})\right\rangle=-\frac{1}{\eta_{1}\eta_{2}}\left\langle G_{z_{1}}(\eta_{1})E_{22}G_{z_{2}}(\eta_{2})E_{22}\right\rangle. $$

Now we use Theorem 3.5 of [15] to approximate this trace by a deterministic quantity

$$ \left\langle H_{z_{1}}(\eta_{1})H_{z_{2}}(\eta_{2})\right\rangle=-\frac{1}{\eta_{1}\eta_{2}}\left\langle\mathcal{B}^{-1}[M_{z_{1}}(\eta_{1})E_{22}M_{z_{2}}(\eta_{2})]E_{22}\right\rangle+\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{N^{-3\epsilon_{0}}}{\eta_{1}\eta_{2}}\right). $$

Here $\mathcal{B}:M_{2N}(\mathbb{C})\rightarrow M_{2N}(\mathbb{C})$ is a linear operator given by

$$ \mathcal{B}(\cdot)=Id-M_{z_{1}}(\eta_{1})\mathcal{S}(\cdot)M_{z_{2}}(\eta_{2}). $$

By a straightforward computation we see that

$$ -\left\langle\mathcal{B}^{-1}[M_{z_{1}}(\eta_{1})E_{22}M_{z_{2}}(\eta_{2})]E_{22}\right\rangle=\frac{|m_{z_{1}}(\eta_{1})m_{z_{2}}(\eta_{2})|}{|1-z_{1}\bar{z_{2}}u_{z_{1}}(\eta_{1})u_{z_{2}}(\eta_{2})|^{2}-m_{z_{1}}(\eta_{1})^{2}m_{z_{2}}(\eta_{2})^{2}}\geq c $$

for some constant $c$ . Here we used that $|m_{z_{j}}(\eta_{j})|$ is bounded below by a constant; for $\eta\geq c_{0}$ for any fixed $c_{0}>0$ , this follows by continuity of solutions to (8.1), and for $\eta\leq c_{0}$ , this follows by Lemma 3.2 in [17] if $c_{0}>0$ is small enough. We also used that the denominator is bounded above by a constant, which can be readily checked using properties of $m_{z_{j}}(\eta_{j})$ , and positive since we know that $\left\langle H_{z_{1}}(\eta_{1})H_{z_{2}}(\eta_{2})\right\rangle>0$ . This concludes the proof of (8.3). The bound (8.4) is proved the same way.

Now we prove (8.5). If $|z_{1}-z_{2}|<N^{-\frac{\epsilon_{0}}{2}}$ , we use Theorem 3.3 of [17] and if $|z_{1}-z_{2}|\geq N^{-\frac{\epsilon_{0}}{2}}$ , we use Theorem 3.5 of [15] to get

$$ \displaystyle\left\langle H_{z_{1}}(\eta_{1})\tilde{H}_{z_{2}}(\eta_{2})\right\rangle \displaystyle=-\frac{1}{\eta_{1}\eta_{2}}\left\langle G_{z_{1}}(\eta_{1})E_{12}G_{z_{2}}(\eta_{2})E_{21}\right\rangle \displaystyle=-\frac{1}{\eta_{1}\eta_{2}}\left\langle\mathcal{B}^{-1}[M_{z_{1}}(\eta_{1})E_{12}M_{z_{2}}(\eta_{2})]E_{21}\right\rangle+\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{N^{\epsilon_{0}}}{N\eta_{\ast}^{2}}\frac{1}{\eta_{1}\eta_{2}}\right). $$

(The quantity $\hat{\beta}_{\ast}$ in Theorem 3.5 of [15] is bounded below uniformly by Lemma 6.1 in [15].) Since $\eta_{\ast}\geq N^{-1/3+\epsilon_{0}}$ , the error term $\mathcal{O}(N^{\epsilon_{0}}N^{-1}\eta_{\ast}^{-4})$ is much smaller than $\eta_{\ast}^{-1}$ . Thus, we can drop the $\mathcal{O}$ -term in the second line. Again, we can directly compute

$$ \displaystyle-\left\langle\mathcal{B}^{-1}[M_{z_{1}}(\eta_{1})E_{12}M_{z_{2}}(\eta_{2})]E_{21}\right\rangle \displaystyle=\frac{|m_{z_{1}}(\eta_{1})m_{z_{2}}(\eta_{2})|\left(1-(|z_{1}|^{2}u_{z_{1}}(\eta_{1})^{2}-m_{z_{1}}(\eta_{1})^{2})(|z_{2}|^{2}u_{z_{2}}(\eta_{2})^{2}-m_{z_{2}}(\eta_{2})^{2})\right)}{|1-z_{1}\bar{z_{2}}u_{z_{1}}(\eta_{1})u_{z_{2}}(\eta_{2})|^{2}-m_{z_{1}}(\eta_{1})^{2}m_{z_{2}}(\eta_{2})^{2}}. $$

Now from the self-consistent equation (8.1) for $m_{z}(\eta)$ , we see that

$$ 0\leq|z|^{2}u_{z}(\eta)^{2}-m_{z}(\eta)^{2}\leq 1-\eta|m_{z}(\eta)|\leq 1-c\eta. $$

Thus

$$ -\left\langle\mathcal{B}^{-1}[M_{z_{1}}(\eta_{1})E_{12}M_{z_{2}}(\eta_{2})]E_{21}\right\rangle\geq c(\eta_{1}+\eta_{2}) $$

for some constant $c$ . The denominator of (8.6) is the determinant of $\mathcal{B}$ . From the calculations in Appendix B of [17] we see that

$$ \det\mathcal{B}\lesssim\eta_{1}+\eta_{2}+|z_{1}-z_{2}|^{2}. $$

This concludes the proof of (8.5). ∎
